subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT STRATEGY-WIDESPREAD COMMODITY AND MATERIAL SHORTAGES
speechtext: Docs the government have a strategy to deal with widespread commodity and materials shortages within Canada which threaten the nation's growth potential for 1974 and, if so, what is the strategy?

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT STRATEGY-WIDESPREAD COMMODITY AND MATERIAL SHORTAGES
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is concerned: Canada moves into the year 1974 after a year of extraordinary high real growth. The world economy, including Canada, has enjoyed three decades of extremely rapid growth by historical standards. Both in a short and rather longerterm sense it is not, therefore, surprising that evidence of specific commodity and material shortages would form a part of the problem of economic management. The tightness of world supply of some commodities and materials has, of course, been exacerbated by the recent major disruptions in petroleum supply. It is anticipated that both material and demand shortages outside of Canada will have a larger influence on Canadian real growth in 1974 than any internal shortages. The government is, however, examining intensively the possibility of strategic shortages particularly in the context of staging major Canadian capital developments over the next decade in a manner which will lead to sustainable growth and minimal dislocation. In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: Officials of the Department of Industry, Trade

and Commerce are fully aware of current and developing situations to do with widespread commodity and materials shortages within Canada. These situations are examined and reviewed regularly on a commodity basis, and options are considered at a time when shortages or future shortages become apparent. The specific action depends on the nature of the commodity and the related industry characteristics. The government is prepared to take whatever steps are required to ensure that Canadians do not suffer unduly as a result of material shortages. In so far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned: The government strategy with respect to ensuring adequate commodity and material supplies was outlined in the throne speech.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN PENSION COMMISSION-APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows: 1. As of 24 February 1974, there were 7,360 applications for pension awaiting decision by the Canadian Pension Commission.
2.	Statistics on outstanding claims are not available for the precise period indicated in the question; however, following are figures for closely related periods as of February 24, 1974: Applications five months or more old, 7,360; Applications twelve months or more old, 5,006; Applications eighteen months or more old, 243.
3.	Most World War I veterans and many World War II veterans for whom decisions on pension application are pending first made unsuccessful applications and exhausted their appeal rights many years ago and before the Pension Act was amended in 1971. For what reason did it take a period of 50 days from September 11, 1973 to October 31, 1973 for the Secretary of State to reply to Question No. 2,671 of the First Session of the 29th Parliament that it was not possible to answer questions as to the total amount of OFY funds allocated in 1972-73 to constituencies represented in the House of Commons by (a) Members of the Liberal Party (b) Members of the Progressive Conservative Party?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: OFY FUNDS TO CONSTITUENCIES REPRESENTED BY LIBERAL AND PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
1.
During the period involved, officials of the Secretary of State Department undertook a Study to examine ways and means of providing the information requested. The findings of the study were that a new computerized structure

would be required to provide information by constituency, and that an inordinate amount of time and expense would be involved in establishing such a structure. For managerial, technical and administrative reasons, the Opportunities for Youth Program and records were built on a regional and subregional basis which did not take into account and did not generally correspond to the actual limits of federal or provincial constituencies. The five regions were Atlantic, Quebec, Ontario, the Prairies and Northwest Territories, and British Columbia and the Yukon.
2.	At the urging of a number of Members of Parliament who had indicated a desire to be consulted on submissions from their own constituencies, the office of the Secretary of State at the beginning of the 1973 program undertook to sort the applications as best it could by federal constituencies. The consultation of April, 1973 did not represent an allocation by constituency, but rather a consultation process by which the Secretary of State gathered information prior to making decisions on projects. In view of the fact that the youth applying for projects were not restricted to being from or operating within one constituency, in multiple-riding urban areas more than one constituency was affected by some proposals. Hence, in many cases, more than one Member of Parliament was consulted. This exercise, arising out of the constituency demand, was not reflected in OFY selection records which are classified by region and subregion. This explains why the 600-page report listing Opportunities for Youth projects for 1973 is classified by provinces, municipalities and localities and in alphabetical order. This document enables a reader who is familiar with the limits of a given constituency to establish a list of those projects which were carried out within that constituency.
3 and 4. It is not possible to answer these questions, since the allocation of the funds of the OFY program was done within a framework of regions and subregions, and not within the framework of electoral constituencies.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: GREAT LAKES-ACTION TO PREVENT FLOODING AND CLEAN UP POLLUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has raised two separate questions. The first deals with flooding on the Great Lakes. With regard to the second question, I was talking today to the chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission who gave me an account of the talks. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS, AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
that Bill C-18, to impose a charge on the export of crude oil and certain petroleum products, to provide compensation for certain oil import costs and to regulate the price of Canadian crude oil in interprovincial and export trade be read the second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill to enact the Petroleum Administration Act provides legislative support for three major themes of government petroleum policy as set forth in the Prime Minister's statement of last December 6 and as put before the first ministers' conference on energy in late January. The agreement which was reached among first ministers on Wednesday, March 27, represented the achievement of a broad consensus among the provinces and the federal government that these themes represent three essential constituents of a national oil policy.
Government policy has developed in response to the major disruptions of world oil markets over the past several months. These disruptions took the form of both temporary restrictions in world supplies of crude oil, and perhaps more importantly in a massive upward movement of world oil prices as producing countries began to exercise monopoly control over world prices.
In response to these forces, government policy has been to articulate three principles: First, that the price of Canadian crude oil should move upward to encourage exploration and development in Canada and thereby ensure further availability of our own resources, which will necessarily be more costly because they are both physically and technically less accessible, and also to ensure a continuing capacity for self-sufficiency. There is no reason why Canadian crude oil must move to interna-

tional levels which no longer represent any fundamental reconciliation of supply and demand in world markets. Second, the approximate one-half of Canadian crude oil production that is exported should be sold at a fair and reasonable opportunity price in United States markets, that is, at a price consistent with the price which the U.S. is paying for other imported oil. Third, the proceeds from the sale of oil in the U.S. at a price higher than the domestic Canadian price should be employed to reduce the exposure of consumers in eastern Canada who would have otherwise had to pay full international prices for oil and oil products. We have described this third principle as embracing a single basic crude oil price to all Canadians except for transportation differentials.
These three themes or principles which, as I have said, have the support of all of the provinces are embodied in this legislation, for which we seek the approval of this House. Part I of this act deals with petroleum export charges, Parts II and III with domestic oil price restraint and Part IV with petroleum import cost compensation.
I believe that by this time the House understands well, Mr. Speaker, the background to the development of this policy. The nationwide address by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on December 6, the statement by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to this House in moving second reading of the Export Tax Act in early January, and the analysis and statements put before first ministers at the energy conference in late January, are all important and comprehensive expressions of both government policy and the reasons for it. If I may say so, Mr. Speaker, while we would make no particular claim for prescience with respect to the rapidly altering world oil scene over the past few months, the record will show that we have been entirely consistent in our view of the policies which Canada would have to adopt in adjusting to these developments.
I would like to review very briefly the major events in this development commencing with September 4 last year. On September 4 the Prime Minister called upon the oil industry, among others, to support a program of voluntary price restraint. This request was part of a general antiinflationary program and was addressed to the oil industry, where crude oil prices had increased by some 95 cents over the previous nine-month period.
It is fair to say that 95 cents looked at the time as a very significant price advance, particularly since world and Canadian crude oil prices prior to these advances had remained relatively stable for more than a decade. Ninety-five cents was, of course, a very modest herald of what was to come. It did nonetheless represent an increase of crude oil price of almost one-third and brought the average price of crude oil and equivalents in western Canada to approximately $3.80 to $3.85 at the wellhead or $4 at Edmonton.
The government's request to the oil industry on September 4 of last year was voluntarily to maintain this average price of crude oil in western Canada and hence the prices of products produced from this crude oil. At that time the government acknowledged that for those refiners dependent on imported oil no such over-all restraint would be
April 8, 1974

possible, and that they would be allowed to pass on documented and approved crude cost increases in the form of higher prices.
When the freeze was instituted, product prices immediately east of the Ottawa Valley line were one cent and two cents lower than those in the west. Eastern gasoline and heating oil prices were permitted to rise by an average of two cents on November 1 and an additional average of five cents on December 1 for which the major tax increases of October 16 in the Middle East and November 1 in Venezuela were principally responsible. These product price movements led to a five cent to six cent differential which has existed in markets served by imported oil since December 1 and will continue to exist until approximately May 15. I will return at a future stage to the events that will occur on or about that date.
Having frozen domestic crude oil prices at $4 at Edmonton, the government was next advised by the National Energy Board in mid-September that continuing increases in international oil prices implied that sales of Canadian crude oil on a $4 basis in United States markets would no longer be just and reasonable nor in the Canadian interest. Rather than permit the industry in Canada to attempt to manage a two-price system from which the benefits would flow exclusively to the industry, the government's immediate response was to give notice that it would seek the approval of this House to levy an export tax equal to the difference between the value of Canadian crude oil delivered in the United States and the average price of all imported oil prevailing in these markets. The export tax, the manner of its imposition and the disposition of its proceeds are now, I am sure, sufficiently well understood, at least as that regime has operated until March 31 of this year, that I need not dwell on it further for the moment.
Nor will I dwell at any length on other developments through this period except to note that government thinking and policy took two broad directions as a result of the exposure of one-half of our country to the increasing difficulties of international oil supply and pricing. The first of these directions was to carry on a very intensive and searching review of Canadian policy with respect to all energy sources. This review led to a series of federal positions which were laid before the first ministers' conference on energy and which have resulted in a continuing and fruitful interchange with provincial authorities in the development of major initiatives in nuclear energy, coal and hydro-electric development and transmission. The second direction was to focus on Canada's oil and gas systems which led, through extensive federal-provincial consultation and the first ministers' conference on energy in January, to the final agreement reached by the first ministers on March 27.
I have already described the origins of the export tax. The imposition of an additional $4 in tax by OPEC countries on January 1, 1974 led quickly to the major decision not to pursue international prices as the pricing norm for Canada. This in turn led to the recognition that, if eastern Canada were to be cushioned from these international prices, then a cost compensation program would be necessary. Finally, the combination of an independent Canadian price and a willingness to pay cost compensation demanded the establishment of a one-price policy country-
Petroleum Administration Act
wide and the eventual elimination of the price differentials that had come to exist between eastern and western Canada.
The most essential element in the establishment of these policies was to settle upon a rational crude oil pricing policy for Canada that would be equitable to both producing and consuming interests and, in the longer term, in the best interest of Canadians. The federal government's central position has been that this price must be such as to ensure the development of Canada's further potential resources, whether in tar sands or frontier areas. We have recognized that the notion of a price which would continue to encourage these developments was conceptually clear but that such a price was and is in fact determined by a host of interdependent factors, many and perhaps most of which are difficult to assess with precision.
We recognized from the outset that reasonable men would differ in their estimate of this price and that a consensus about it would only emerge from an intensive process of analysis and discussion. We recognized, of course, also that the level of this price had major implications for producing provinces and their right to a return from this depleting resource to ensure their continuing development and prosperity. At the same time a very substantive upward movement in price would represent a very major transfer of income from consumers of Canadian oil. We have always been mindful as well of the consequences for the Canadian economy of a sharp advance in the price of crude oil and the structural readjustments and inflationary problems it would pose.
In retrospect, while the differences that have emerged in this consultative process have occasionally seemed sharp and irreconcilable, I would like to join with the Prime Minister in asserting that federalism triumphed in reaching a solution to a problem which was at its heart a matter of relative equities and sharing within our country.

speechtext: Thank God for Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS, AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Thank God for Alberta, sir, and for the other nine provinces. My presentation to the first ministers' conference in January and the table of a possible distribution of costs and benefits which I presented at that time have in fact set the pattern within which this solution was reached. That pattern assures a restrained price to consumers, an increase in return to producing provinces, a limitation on increase in general equalization payments which would otherwise have fallen on the general taxpayer, and a specialized kind of equalization; that is, the oil-cost cushion for the benefit of eastern Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces.
Let me now move to the agreements which were reached among the first ministers on March 27 and, in the process, I hope, clear up any misunderstandings which may yet remain in respect of the policy which will be followed in this country over the next 12 to 15-month period.
In a matter as technically complex as oil which flows from many origins and in many qualities it is always risky to speak of averages. Averages may be struck at various times and various places and produce very different results. In continuously speaking of the frozen price of
1236

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
western crude as having an average value of $4 we have always tried to be clear that this average was struck with regard to oil at Edmonton. Embraced within this definition of oil is conventional crude, synthetic crude oil and two naptha-like liquids called condensate and pentanes plus which are most frequently blended in the crude stream which flows from Edmonton.
We have always tried also to be clear that this average if struck at the well-head broadly defined and not at Edmonton would approximate $3.85. The difference between these two figures represents the average gathering charges to move oil from its source to its major gathering points.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his statement to the press on the evening of March 27, and in his statement to this House on March 28, made it quite clear that the agreement specified a $6.50 average well-head price. A further explanation of the details to the House generally was interrupted by hon. members, but the Prime Minister explained these to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield).
On March 28 Premier Lougheed announced his understanding of a $6.50 well-head price as involving an increase of $2.70, apparently basing his calculations on conventional crude prices alone. I regret that there was no consultation with us because quite frankly our own estimate of the amount needed to be added on to achieve a $6.50 average well-head price was $2.65. We recognize that a precise measure of this average is difficult to arrive at for the reasons I have already mentioned, though we would have liked an opportunity to consult further with Alberta officials in order to remove all misunderstanding. We have, however, acknowledged in this House that the difference between $2.70 and $2.65 arises from a misunderstanding, but it is not a point fundamental to the major policy understanding accepted by the premiers on March 27 last and, therefore, not an issue which we wish to press further at this time.
In summary then, all western crude and equivalent prices rose by $2.70 on April 1, leading to an average price of $6.70 based on Edmonton and $7.20 delivered in Toronto. Given our intention to zone the major markets in Toronto and Montreal for crude pricing purposes when the Sarnia-Montreal pipeline is in place, we are also employing $7.20 as the basic price in Montreal on which cost compensation will be paid. As the House is aware, I have asked the industry to refrain from passing on these higher crude ' costs in higher product prices until a substantial proportion of their lower cost inventories have been worked off. In 45 days, however, product prices may be expected to rise by approximately eight cents west of the old Ottawa Valley line and three cents east of that line to establish approximate product price equality in Montreal and Toronto on that date.
First ministers also agreed that the federal government should receive all of the proceeds from export charges on oil in order to permit it to provide the substantial amount of cost compensation which will be required in eastern Canada to maintain the one-price concept. In committee, I shall provide this House with estimates of the sums involved.
I would note at this time that the petroleum export charge section of the legislation before us today proposes

the levy of an export charge on both the broad definition of crude oil as defined under the Export Tax Act and on oil products to be specified by regulation. The absence of a charge on products has meant that exports in that form have not borne their share of taxation. Now that an agreement has been reached for 12 to 15 months and the major principles of a national oil policy have been laid in place it is important to move to close this possible loophole of tax avoidance.
Finally, I should like to give the House notice that I shall be moving in committee to amend the $4.20 export charge for April to read $4. The $4.20 recorded in the legislation was arrived at when we were basing our calculations on the averaged price for oil at Edmonton. These calculations will now be made on an averaged well-head price which does not include transportation charges for delivery to Edmonton.
Part II of this act entitled "Domestic Oil Price Restraint" legislates a federal authority over crude oil pricing in interprovincial and export trade and provides the mechanism by which the agreement reached with the provinces can be ratified by the federal government.
Part III of the act, which we do not intend to proclaim at this time, provides a solely federal mechanism for maintaining control of crude prices in interprovincial and export trade should it at some time be required. This could happen if challenges to provincial legislation by private litigants, like those now in the courts, are successful or in other ways such as the failure of agreement on prices in the future. In these or similar eventualities it will be essential to have a federal mechanism which can take the place of provisions under Part II.
Parts IV and V set forth the terms, conditions and measures by which the Energy Supplies Allocation Board will act as the government's agent in administering the import cost compensation program. As the House is aware, shipments of crude oil eligible for compensation into early March have been covered by supplementary vote in the fiscal year 1973-74 and the program is being administered by my department. The legislation before the House today provides a transitional mechanism to permit the Energy Supplies Allocation Board to assume obligations arising out of the first quarter but not covered by the supplementary vote.
The governor in council will this week approve regulations with regard to the earlier period which will limit the amount of compensation that will be paid for identifiable increases in post-government taxes, increased bunker costs of transport and a provision for retroactive increases in cost which may occur as a result of increasing host government ownership of the producing companies.
It is the government's intention, as will be clear from the legislation, to embody this same set of principles in providing compensation after April 1. I would remind the House that at the present time the federal government has no power, nor does it intend to seek power, to control product prices down to the retail level. Several provinces have already acted to cushion the effect on consumers at the retail level. Nonetheless, extensive monitoring and auditing provisions are provided under this legislation to ensure that refiners who receive compensation are follow-
April 8, 1974

ing wholesale pricing practices which are consistent with this compensation.
I would only conclude by saying that this is a very important piece of legislation in the evolution of national oil policy. It provides the legislative support which will be required to maintain these national policies, national policies which as I have said have received the concurrence of all the provinces and, I believe, of the Canadian people generally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the minister at the outset of my remarks in saying how glad we were to see the first ministers arrive at some form of consensus. That does not mean necessarily that we approve of everything in that consensus. I believe this is one of the few occasions when the first ministers did get together and work out a form of agreement, but what bludgeons, what blackmail, what advantages, what favours or what anaesthetics were administered during that meeting I do not know. At least it was a meeting which resulted in some decisions being arrived at, and I am glad for that reason.
I want to say through you, Mr. Speaker, to members of this House that it is our view, and certainly it is mine, that merely because the provincial and federal governments arrived at a decision is no reason that this House, this parliament and certainly not this party should rubber-stamp and accept without challenge, without examination and without the closest possible legal study, the results which were arrived at. We must ensure that the results which were in fact arrived at at that meeting are implemented in this legislation.
The minister quite glibly told us that everything in this bill is the result of the federal-provincial conference. We are not so sure about that. My friend, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) asked a very searching question today. As I think was his duty, not knowing what the answer would be, he asked the minister whether there had been discussions with the provinces following the first ministers' conference and whether this bill in fact represents the views they have considering what should be in the bill as a result of their discussions. The minister did not answer that question. He could not answer it. In fact he said that they decided in cabinet what would be done, implemented it in legislative form, brought it down and gave it first reading. Now, it is up to the provinces to look at it and decide. As a result, it will be our intention to make very certain during the committee meetings before this bill receives final approval, and certainly before it receives third reading, that there is ample opportunity for the provincial representatives and others to examine the legislation to make certain it in fact contains the arrangement arrived at at this first minister's conference.

The federal government stands across the way shivering, shaking and trembling in the fear that it will be forced into an election before too long by some unnamed parties in this House which I will not mention at this time. There is nothing wrong with this, but we must remember that when the leaders or the 11 heads of government get together to consider what they propose to do they take into consideration in their calculations what the benefits are to their governments in the prosecution of an election. I think for that and other reasons it is incumbent upon this House, despite the fact that there has been the seal of approval placed upon the agreement, not necessarily upon this bill, to ascertain that the bill does in fact conform with what was agreed upon and then even if it does to consider whether it is good for all parts of Canada. That is our duty and I do not intend to be intimidated by the minister from the exercise of that duty and responsibility.
Let us make a quick analysis of the bill, because I do not think I need to take too long to deal with it. Unlike other bills, it is divided into five parts instead of three. The first part, as the minister told us, deals with the question of the tax or charge. He calls it a petroleum export charge. I do not think the name matters a great deal; it smells just as sweet by any name. Then, parts II and III complement each other and deal with price fixing mechanisms for

petroleum and petroleum products in Canada. Part IV deals with the compensation to importers to provide some cushion for consumers in eastern Canada as a result of the high prices which they have had to pay for oil coming in from overseas. Part V, of course, is a procedural section.
I want to say that when you look at all the clauses in the bill you find that some very far-reaching powers and authorities are granted in it to the federal government, powers which I do not think have ever been granted in peacetime to a federal government. I went through the bill and I found that it contains 66 clauses of which two or three are purely functional but 22 give complete discretion to either the government, the governor in council, boards or the minister. In other words, more than one third of the clauses vest in the government substantial uncontrolled discretionary powers. In addition to that, there are four regulation granting clauses which in 24 instances grant the power to the governor in council to act by regulation and order in council. This indicates the very substantial extent to which we are being asked in the bill to trust this government with its sorry and chequered history of starts and stops, reverses, mistakes and errors with regard to the whole problem of petroleum products going years back from the time when this government was asked by members of this party and members of the NDP to look to the future and build a pipeline from western Canada to Montreal. This plea was rejected with laughter and scorn by the Liberal government right up to the most recent mess, the great mystery about the Roumanian oil which has yet to be solved in the House in which the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer)-otherwise known as the minister of everything else-and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) got this country into a pretty sorry pickle as a result of which we will lose some $30 million. $40 million or $50 million dollars.
This is the government which is asking us to calmly and confidently vest in it all these extraordinary powers which are contained and itemized in this bill. This is the government which, in the words of the minister a few minutes ago, had such great prescience in anticipating all the problems with regard to the oil and petroleum industry. What a farce, what a sham for this minister to have the unmitigated gall to rise in the House and say that he and the government have been able to anticipate the twistings, turnings and problems with regard to the petroleum industry in Canada. I think it is shameful for the minister to take that position. As a matter of fact, although I do not have much time, I will go through some of the items because I suspect that the minister would appropriate to himself this degree of perfection in connection with his dealings with petroleum products.
I find the following item in the Toronto Star of May 7 of 1973; "Prime Minister says Ottawa should not control our energy prices". Only a year ago this great Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) of this great government had the supernatural powers to anticipate what will happen!
I find here another interesting item in the Globe and Mail of November 5, 1973 which reads: "Macdonald denies urging cabinet to buy oil firm". We know all of the comings, goings and leakings which went on at that time about the government wanting to buy one of the great multinational oil firms, taking it over and operating it.

In a statement issued on Saturday, Mr. Macdonald described as "entirely erroneous" a Globe and Mail report that the cabinet had rejected his proposal to buy either Shell Canada Limited or Gulf Oil Canada Limited. He said no such proposal was placed before cabinet.
There is a different story behind that, I believe.
Then, we have the following item: "Secret cabinet order waters down plans for energy policy". That was the leaked cabinet order by which we learned the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources ascertained that his proposals had been watered down by the federal cabinet and that what he had proposed was not going to be brought about at all.
Then, he was over in Venezuela, and here I have the March 9, 1974 issue of the Winnipeg Free Press in which the following item appears: "Is Ottawa about to copy the Corporacion Venezolana de Petroleo ..." Perhaps the minister will correct my Spanish. I hope he is better in Spanish than he is on petroleum. It goes on to read:
Energy Minister Donald S. Macdonald, here last October on a whirlwind visit, says definitely no.
They are not going to have a petroleum corporation, he said.
The cabinet discussed the idea before the energy crisis took hold, says our energy minister, and before the Canadian government started to worry about supplies of Venezuelan crude oil going to eastern Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS, AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
I would have preferred if the minister had introduced Parts I and IV of the bill dealing with the imposition of the charge and compensation payments. So far as we are concerned they could be passed fairly rapidly, submitted to committee of the whole, and completed. They have been the subject of practice and precedent. If my recollection is correct the minister and the government have engaged in the imposition of the charge for four months without benefit of legislation, and for several months the government has paid the subsidy without benefit of legislation. With some scrutiny, some changes and some recommendations, Parts I and IV might have gone through rapidly if they had been separated from the rest of the legislation. However, the government has not seen fit to do so. That is its practice, and of course it has that right. But the other parts of the bill warrant far more detailed study in the House and, so far as we in this party are concerned, we will see they get that.
Now, dealing with Part I, this export tax or charge is a comparatively recent phenomenon, at least to the large extent to which it is being engaged in presently by this country and other countries. We are not going to challenge it. We are not going to vote against it. However, I think I would be wrong if I did not call attention to some of the potential dangers regarding a charge of this kind, and if I did not speak about the entire philosophy of the export tax, its morality, and its being a double edged sword. Where does it stop?
All over the world we hear talk of other countries, producing commodities which are in short supply, feeling free to engage in a form of international arrangement, such as the OPEC countries have, denying the world a full, assured supply of those commodities. The Arab OPEC countries were the first to raise this question. Maybe they had a point. I could understand them when they said that all the civilized countries of the world were gripped in inflation, and they would meet that inflation by imposing higher charges for petroleum products from their countries, petroleum which was in decreasing supply and which cannot be self-perpetuating. The Arab countries said to the western world, "Search yourselves. Find ways and means of dealing with inflation. Then, we will give some thought to reducing the cost of our petroleum products." I think that needed to be said, but we have to be aware of the effect on international inflation.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) shrug their shoulders and say, "We cannot deal with inflation in Canada. It is worldwide in scope." That may be true enough in part, but there are substantial elements of it within Canadian control, just as

there are substantial elements within the control of OPEC countries and within the control of other countries.
If all the countries of the world took the same position as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and said, "This is worldwide. We cannot touch it," that would constitute a very serious admission that inflation lies entirely outside the control of mankind. I do not think that is right. I think man has the capacity and ability on a co-operative basis, both nationally and internationally, to deal with the problem of inflation. I am not going to take exception to what is being done here, but I do say that at the time of passage of this particular part of the bill we should give serious concern to what could happen to the world with a series of export charges levied by producing countries, the combined effect of which could be felt not only in Canada directly but in an indirect way through the cost of the products which ultimately come to this country.
Mr. Speaker, I like to think that neither I nor my party have any quarrel with the principle that sudden, unexpected and unusual, windfall profits which accrue to companies should be shared by society. However, that statement has to be taken in conjunction with our belief in free, private initiative and enterprise as the best way to develop this country. We believe that such charges must take into calculation the need to provide for continuation of these companies in business and to provide them with adequate funds to carry on exploration, development, refining and marketing of their product. It then becomes a question of sharing those windfall profits but to the extent that they constitute an unearned increment, then I think the state is entitled to share in them. For that reason this party will not challenge this aspect of the legislation. The whole question of unearned income has not been given enough thought in this regard or in regard to a number of other things.
We are in a desperate position in this country with regard to the sale of land because we have allowed such sales without taking into account that there are substantial unearned increments involved which should belong to the state. But certainly you must give, and in doing so it must be contemporaneous with giving to the private sector, the tools and weapons to do the work that they can do better than the public or government. I refer to the things which attract them and, in this particular aspect context, I refer to the exploration, the development, refining and marketing of petroleum products. We have no objection to that. We are concerned to some extent with the way the clauses are drawn which give effect to that proposal.
Part of the clauses I refer to give very wide and vast powers of discretion to the government in dealing with exemption from this charge. For example, clause 11 in Part I provides that the Governor in Council can, on being advised by the board that it is in the public interest to do so, either generally or in respect of a single transaction, exempt any exportation of oil from the charge imposed thereon in respect of any month. Now, by Part I, after the month of April has elapsed, we are giving to the government the power to impose a charge of up to $8 per barrel, solely within the discretion of the government flowing
April 8, 1974

from rudimentary and wide terms of reference. At the same time we are giving the government the power to exempt imposition of that export charge.
I recognize that it is neither possible, feasible nor wise, to bring back legislation of this kind and have it dealt with two or three times per year, but I am going to suggest that when we are forced to give that kind of discretionary power to a government, including the right to give exemptions, there should be an accounting to this House. It is not good enough that once a year the minister brings in a report which may come 1 lA years after the event. I would like to think that during the committee hearing our party would propose an amendment whereby the boards involved in this legislation, and the minister, will be required to account to a committee of this House charged with a special responsibility with regard to legislation of this kind. This would permit the people of Canada, acting through members of this House, by a committee, to examine, for example, why charges have been fixed at a certain rate; and, if the government sees fit to give exemption of one company or one type of petroleum product for a substantial sum, why this was done. I am not saying that the government would act illegally or unwisely but I suggest that it is a far, far better thing for a government to know that it will be subject to close and searching examination by a committee of this House from time to time as to the use of the uncontrolled, discretionary powers of this House.
The same generally applies to Part IV of this bill, the import cost compensation. This is a discretionary amount and is covered in clauses 51, 52 and 53. Clause 51 says that the import cost compensation may be paid to an eligible importer. He is defined as a person who at a certain stage has voluntarily maintained a level of prices for petroleum products obtained from imported petroleum at the level suggested in prescribed manner, and so on. Clause 54 goes on to say that there may be special cases where in the discretion of the board which has been indicated to the government of Canada that:
... the board may, if it is of the opinion, that it is in the public interest to do so, recommend to the government of Canada that an additional amount of compensation be authorized for the importer in respect of that petroleum.
There may be some cases where that is justified, but I would think that where you give to any government the power to impose a tax at a fixed rate, but a flexible tax, at its discretion, a tax which may vary from month to month and at the same time give to that government the right to exempt certain people from the effect of that tax, then the House should retain some form of supervision over what is done.
Let me deal briefly with Parts II and III of the bill, Mr. Speaker. Those are the parts which constitute the price fixing mechanism. The government and the minister may call it what they want, but there is no doubt that this is a mechanism for fixing prices in Canada with regard to petroleum products. It is set out quite clearly in clause 20 as follows:
The purpose of this part is to provide legislative authority for measures that will, so far as may be practicable, enable the government of Canada
(a) to achieve a uniform price,-
Petroleum, Administration Act
That is a laudable objective. I am not quarrelling with it and I am not going to challenge it on a constitutional ground but I point out to the minister, to the government and to members of this House that there are very grave doubts about how far a federal government may go in establishing, through these means, a price fixing mechanism in this country. This House is not the forum for dealing with constitutional cases and I do not want to do so, but it is possible that those aspects of the bill may be challenged at some time. It seems to me, however, and this is purely a private opinion, that there were other mechanisms which might have been adopted.
Price fixing lies exclusively within provincial jurisdiction. Just thinking out loud, for the life of me I cannot see why the consuming provinces do not take upon themselves the responsibility of establishing a price which they consider to be, in effect, the price fixed by the agreement. The agreement was made; they arrived at a price. Say the $6.70 which the minister referred to was a reasonable price, now the minister and the government have seen fit to introduce federal legislation of some doubtful constitutional character. I think there were other means by which it could have been done. Certainly, the province could have done it and it could not have been challenged. It is certainly in the interests of the consuming provinces to implement the federal-provincial agreement in a legislative form or, if they desire, in another form. There are suggestions in this bill. Clauses 21 and 22 state an agreement can be arrived at between the federal and provincial governments. It goes on to state that agreement will be implemented.
It is well-known constitutional law that one government cannot delegate authority to another government. That was held in one case in particular dealing with a marketing board in Prince Edward Island. Dickens said the law is an ass. Probably it is at times. However, the Supreme Court went on to say you can delegate to a Crown corporation or an emanation of the government. If the federal government and the provincial governments arrived at a reasonable arrangement which they found acceptable, if they arrived at a mechanism whereby they did not see fit to consider the establishment of a Crown corporation, an emanation or a board, it would have the right to receive from both federal and provincial authorities the jurisdiction it requires to exercise this price fixing mechanism. I point that out as I go through and look at these sections.
There is someone else complaining about the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this measure, Bill C-18, is very complex. As hon. members have stated, it consists of five parts. Part I deals with the imposition of the export charge. Part II gives statutory expression to the agreement which was reached at the first ministers conference on Wednesday, March 27.
Part III is to be the sword of Damocles which will hang over the heads of the oil-producing provinces. If they do not reach a voluntary agreement by June 30, 1975, Part III can be proclaimed and the federal government will have the power to set the price for oil. I think that ultimately the federal government must have such power. Whether passing such a provision now is going to create the most friendly atmosphere in which negotiations can be carried on, I very much doubt.
Part IV provides for compensation to the companies for oil imported into eastern Canada. Part V is merely a general section dealing with inspection and penalties for non-compliance. Actually, Part I of this bill is a tax act. The other parts have to do with price fixing and a basis for payments of compensation.
I hope that the minister and the House will give some thought whether or not the whole bill should be treated as a tax bill. If I understood the speaker correctly when he was proposing the bill, he said it would go to committee of the whole. This will preclude the calling of witnesses. It will preclude a detailed examination by a committee which will have more time than the committee of the whole. Therefore, I hope the government and the House will give consideration to sending this bill to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
One can only examine this bill if one does so within the framework of a national oil policy. We have been waiting for a long time for a statement from the government on a national oil policy. We have been promised it for a long time. Last June we finally got the first volume of a national policy. It was an analysis, not containing recom-

mendations with respect to an oil policy. We have had great difficulty knowing what is the government's oil policy.
I want to make clear that as far as the New Democratic Party is concerned, we have stated in this House and have presented resolutions to the House setting forth what we think ought to be the major planks in a national oil policy.
As early as January 9, 1973, we were pressing the government for export controls on crude oil. On Monday, May 28,1 introduced a motion on behalf of the New Democratic Party. In that motion and the debate that followed, we asked the government to place export controls on crude oil and petroleum products. We asked for the establishment of a two-price system for crude oil and petroleum products. We asked for an export tax which would take into the public treasury of the federal and provincial governments the difference between the domestic price and the export price. We called for the removal of the Borden Line through the Ottawa Valley.
On October 25, another allotted day, I moved on behalf of this party a resolution calling for a national petroleum company that would be the sole purchaser of both domestically produced oil and imported oil. We pressed for the extension of the oil pipeline to eastern Canada and the bringing of the Interprovincial Pipeline under federal ownership. We also pressed the federal government to enter into negotiations with the government of oil producing provinces with a view to developing, if agreeable, the oil sands under a joint federal-provincial Crown corporation.
The first thing I want to say about this bill is that it is a very firm commitment to a two-price system for oil. While one may disagree with some of the methods proposed- and I certainly disagree with some of the means by which the government proposes to implement this agreement-I think the government is to be commended for taking these steps, which began on November 4, 1973 to implement a two-price system in Canada.
This raises the whole question as to why a two-price system is not to be applied to other Canadian resource materials whose prices are also being escalated by world demand. I think most people in western Canada support the principle of a two-price system. But surely they have some justification when they complain that the only two commodities which are subject to a two-price system are oil and wheat, the two commodities upon which they depend for a very large part of their income.

speechtext:
The minister says, copper. Yes, I think there is some restriction applied to copper but as I recollect there is no export tax to take up the price differential, so it does not help very much.
We have talked a great deal in this House about inflation. Inflation is undoubtedly a major problem affecting every country in the world. No nation has been able to develop an antibiotic which will cure this contagious infection but some nations have been able to cushion the shock of rising prices better than others. We all recognize
April 8, 1974

we cannot control the prices of goods imported into this country, goods we do not produce here-citrus fruits, bauxite, coffee, natural rubber and so on. But we can protect Canadian consumers against the escalating prices of materials produced in this country, particularly those goods in respect of which world demand is pushing prices far beyond a reasonable return to those who produce them.
One of the reasons I differ from hon. members of the Progressive Conservative Party when they talk about a price freeze across the board, is this: if you freeze the price of lumber the main result will be that Canadians will not get any lumber, because if the world price is higher than the price you have fixed the lumber will go out of the country. If we intend to grapple with inflation in this country we should be prepared to treat a number of other commodities in the same way as we propose to treat oil under the legislation before us, that is to impose export controls, fix a domestic price, sell at the world price and pick up for the public treasury the differential between the two prices.
The second matter I wish to discuss arising from this legislation is the pricing policy established in parts of II and III of the bill. The position of the New Democratic Party has been that there is absolutely no justification for giving the oil companies returns higher than those they are now receiving. Prior to the price freeze on September 4 last, the oil companies had already increased their price by approximately one dollar a barrel. This brought them additional revenue amounting to more than $700 million a year. That they are not suffering is shown by the fact that in 1973 they increased their profits by approximately 46 per cent as compared with 1972. One company, for instance, Shell Oil, increased its profits by 58 per cent. Throughout this discussion the NDP has emphasized that the only justification for increasing oil prices is the need to provide funds to federal and provincial governments to enable them to develop new sources of oil so as to ensure adequate supplies when our present proven reserves are exhausted. We believe consumers would not mind being called upon to pay a little more for gasoline and home heating oil if by doing so they could be assured of future supplies at reasonable prices, and knowing they would not be left at the tender mercies of the oil exporting countries and the multinational corporations. But there is nothing in the legislation before us to ensure that the additional funds being received from Canadians will be used for the development of our resources by Canadians, for Canadians.
Reading some newspaper editorials one gathers the impression that the increase of $2.50 a barrel proposed as a result of the first ministers conference constitutes a rip-off on the part of the oil producing provinces. Let me point out that the oil producing provinces will be no better off under the pricing system proposed in this bill than they were under the voluntary agreement which expired on March 31. For instance, Saskatchewan was getting $5 a barrel. In addition, the province was receiving 50 per cent of the export tax, which worked out at approximately $1.60 averaged over their entire production. This gave the province $6.60 a barrel. Now, they are to get $6.50 a barrel. The government of Saskatchewan has set up a petroleum company which purchases the oil from the producers. It is going to pay the oil companies $3.38 a barrel. The differ-
Petroleum Administration Act
ence between that amount and the $6.50 will go into the treasury to give the government the necessary capital for the development of oil supplies which have not yet been fully exploited, and for exploration to discover new sources.
The Province of Alberta was getting $4 a barrel for its oil. It received $1.60 as its share of the export tax, which brought the price up to $5.60. It would now get $6.50. But the Province of Alberta is sharing the $2.50 increase with the oil companies, the government taking 65 per cent and the oil companies 35 per cent. In other words, the oil companies will get 88 cents and the government of Alberta will get $1.62. This will mean an increase in revenue for the oil companies in Alberta of approximately $525 million a year, not counting some of the additional concessions which the minister now appears to be giving them.
On March 27, announcing that this agreement had been reached, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said: "This is a great day for Canadian federalism". I suggest it was a great day for the multinational oil companies. They are going to do very well out of this agreement.
Today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that there has been a good deal of confusion as to what the price would be under this agreement. I do not know anybody who has been more confused than the minister. When the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) met the press at a press conference on March 27, the following question by the press, which I take from the transcript, was asked:
-what does this mean in terms of domestic price increases for home heating oil and also for gasoline at the gas station?
The minister replied:
-basically in terms of feedstock, we're talking 7 cents west of the Ottawa Valley line and I would think the price should probably remain flat in Montreal and in the east.
It did not remain flat for very long, Mr. Speaker. The next day the minister announced that the price increase would be seven cents per gallon west of the Ottawa Valley and three cents a gallon east of the Ottawa Valley. At the same time the minister sent out a Telex to the oil industry in which he told them that the government was prepared to allow them to raise their retail prices to cover any increased cost of refining, etc.

One of the strange things about this pricing mechanism is that we are being asked to approve it although there is no written agreement. Clause 21 of the bill makes reference to an agreement, but goes on to provide that the agreement need not be expressed in any formal document, that the agreement can be contained in reciprocal orders in council. We can discuss this matter later, but I want to point out now that neither this House nor any committee of this House should be asked to pass legislation giving authority to the government to impose a price mechanism on the basis of an agreement that we have not seen and of reciprocal orders in council that have not been tabled. This I hope the minister will do before this bill is dealt with any further.
The fact is that the oil provinces have not gained by this increase of $2.50 per barrel. As I have said, the province of Saskatchewan will be getting slightly less than it was getting before. I believe the government could have kept the price of gasoline and home heating fuels down for the consumers of Canada by giving to the producing provinces a lower price and part of the revenue received from the export charge. The government could quite easily set the price at $5 per barrel, which would have meant an increase of only three cents a gallon for gasoline and home heating fuel, and given the provinces a share of the export tax. Of course, had the government done this it would have meant less revenue for the federal government and a good deal less revenue for the multinational oil companies that control over 90 per cent of the oil business in this country.
The third matter I want to turn to is Part IV of the bill which provides for payments to the oil industry to compensate them for the cost of oil imported into eastern Canada. The New Democratic Party has all along favoured an equalized price across Canada, plus transportation costs, but I must say I have very serious reservations about the manner in which the government is seeking to do this. I do not believe that the burden for equalizing prices should be placed entirely upon the oil consumers, especially where the price of oil enters into the cost of production of farmers, fishermen, the trucking industry and many other groups.

This tax to compensate the oil companies bears no relationship whatsoever to ability to pay. The mere fact that farmers consume per capita more petroleum products than any other group in the country, that fishermen have to buy large quantities of oil, that men in my constituency have to drive 50 to 60 miles to logging camps and sawmills every day, that dock workers have to buy gasoline to enable them to move from port to port, has no relationship to the ability of these workers to pay. The burden of financing compensation in order to have an equalized price across Canada should not fall on any single class of person or on any specific region of Canada but ought to be spread across all of Canada and based upon the ability to pay. The purpose of this provision is to enable the government to pay the oil companies for imported oil which, of course, will be much more expensive than the $6.50 price being fixed by this legislation. The minister says it will cost $1.4 billion.
It is interesting to see how the oil companies are to be compensated. They are to be compensated first of all for increased costs attributable to increased taxes or royalties imposed by producing oil countries. Secondly, they are to be compensated for increased costs attributable to increased participation costs imposed by producing countries and, finally, they are to be compensated for increased tanker costs.
What this parliament is being asked to do is undertake to pay the oil industry for increased costs that are completely beyond Canadian control and, even more seriously, completely beyond our ability to inspect, the books of the foreign companies, to find out whether these costs are genuine or fictitious. This legislation could be an open invitation to oil producing countries to raise their royalties and impose participation costs. Many of the oil companies own their own tankers, and this could be an invitation to raise, on their books at least, the transportation costs. In my opinion this provision could prove to be the greatest rip-off since the CPR went on government welfare. When I consider the business acumen which has been displayed by the Gold Dust twins in negotiating the purchase of home heating oil I shudder to think of the fleecing which the Canadian taxpayer could receive from an industry that is already bloated with the profits it has made out of this so-called oil crisis.
The NDP has constantly advocated the setting up of a national petroleum company to be the sole purchaser of both domestic and imported oil. We have urged the government to enter into bilateral agreements with oil producing countries so as to avoid the kind of rip-off which all too apparently could be possible under this legislation.
The government is being compelled to raise the price of oil for all Canadian consumers so as to compensate the oil companies for standardizing prices in eastern Canada. The consumers of this country are being asked to pay for the mistakes of succeeding governments in following a policy for years of exporting half of our oil to the United States and leaving eastern Canada without an assured supply of oil, completely at the tender mercies of the oil producing countries and the multinational oil corporations. The chickens have come home to roost and it is the Canadian consumer who is now going to be asked to feed them.

In conclusion, let me say that there is nothing in this legislation which will prepare Canada for the real oil crisis that we will face within the next decade. We are dealing with a diminishing asset whose life index is only
10	or 12 years. We want to know in this setup as envisaged in Bill C-18 what role there is for the national petroleum company the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced on December 6 last. Will it have any role in marketing? Will it have any role in developing south of the 60th parallel, or is it to be restricted to birddogging for the multi-national
011	companies by using tax dollars for research and for exploration, turning its findings over to the oil industry? From the minister's explanation so far one gathers that the national petroleum company, if it sees the light of day, will be largely peripheral and will have no really effective role to play in the oil policy this government is evolving on a hit-and-miss basis.
What is the government's policy for developing the oil sands and heavy oil in western Canada? The amount of money being made available to the oil producing provinces under this legislation will not enable those provinces to develop those oil sands. How do we propose to develop them? Is it proposed that we develop them in the same way we developed the conventional oil fields, allowing the multi-national companies to come in and take the oil so that we lose control of it, or has the government some other plan in mind? I am told that last fall Mr. Herman Kahn of the Hudson Institute had at least one or two meetings with government to sell his idea of borrowing $20 billion in foreign capital to build 10 plants in the Athabasca oil sands, and to pay back that $20 billion, plus interest, I assume, in oil. This means that we are proposing out of the Athabasca oil sands to earmark between $20 billion and $30 billion worth of oil to foreign countries without any regard to our own needs or the future needs of our children.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REDUCTION IN FARE STRUCTURE OF NEWFOUNDLAND FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of reducing the present passenger-car fare and freight rate structure of the North Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Port-aux-Basques and Argentia, Newfoundland ferry service to better conform with the cost of travelling a comparable distance on the Trans-Canada highway system as a more economic link between the province and the mainland of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be given the opportunity to present this motion. Indeed, I might say that the subject matter of the motion is by no means new to this chamber nor was it new to the last Parliament. On

November 1, 1968 during my maiden speech in the House of Commons, I requested that the government consider the advisability of reducing the present passenger car fare and freight rate structure of the North Sydney-Port-aux-Basques-Argentia ferry service to better conform with the cost of travelling a comparable distance on the trans-Canada highway system.
Today, almost six years later, I am still doing the same thing. Needless to say, Sir, it becomes extremely frustrating to speak about the same problem time and time again, make the same request year after year and have governments treat the problem with their usual complete lack of interest and total indifference. The province of Newfoundland, with the exception of Labrador, is an island province. The ferry service to which I have referred is the only link it has with the mainland of Canada except, of course, by two airline services operating in and out of the province. I think Your Honour will appreciate the importance of my motion in that it stands to reason the 90 miles of water separating this province from the rest of Canada is to us what the trans-Canada highway system is to people living in the other nine provinces. I contend that, for purposes of a passenger-car and freight rate structure, we should not be treated any differently from the other provinces.
In 1949, Newfoundland elected to become a province of Canada. In so doing we brought to this country a wealth of people and a wealth of resources. As a result of our union, Canada became one of the largest land masses in the world joined from sea to sea. Ironically enough, our geographic position, the fact that we enabled Canada to round out confederation and to become a nation stretching from one sea to another, has been the greatest contributing factor in our ability, or perhaps I should say in our inability, to achieve our full potential and to make confederation really meaningful to a large segment of our population.
As part of the terms of union between our two countries, it was agreed that Canada would take over certain services and from that date relieve the province of Newfoundland of the cost incurred in respect of these services, including the then Newfoundland railway which of course included the coastal fleet and other marine services in the province. Twenty years later, in 1969 or 1970, we saw the Canadian government abolish our rail passenger service and commence its deliberate plan to downgrade and, I suspect, eventually phase out altogether certain other marine services, including the coastal fleet. Of course, this was done by the Canadian National Railways with the concurrence of the Canadian Transport Commission and that of the federal government. Having said that, the question arises: How long can we expect to have a ferry service? That question is not as far fetched as it might sound, because who would have thought, back in 1949 including the people who negotiated our terms of union that 20 years from that date the Canadian government and CNR would abandon our rail passenger service? Could any of us in those days have imagined that one day our coastal fleet would be reduced to a mere fraction of what it was at the time of union?
I will not repeat the story of the rail passenger service in our province, which has been abandoned. We have men-
April 8, 1974

tioned this on numerous occasions. My colleagues from Newfoundland and I have brought this matter to the attention of the House and of the government, but unfortunately our pleas have fallen on deaf ears. Suffice it to say that the service was abandoned with the full knowledge of the CNR and the concurrence of the federal government and its agency the Canadian Transport Commission. We might ask ourselves what changes are contemplated by the new organization which was recently established to administer the ferry service in eastern Canada. Will they follow the example of Canadian National Railways and be more concerned with balance-sheets, profit, losses and subsidies than they will with providing this essential service to our people?
I know that we will hear from members on the other side about the substantial subsidies that are granted by the Canadian government for the operation of the ferry service. We will be told by some hon. members opposite that services costing "X" numbers of dollars have been subsidized every year to the tune of so many millions of dollars. Surely that cannot be the criterion used by this government for the provision of an essential and fundamental public service to our province. I do not think that the government should be any more concerned with the cost of subsidizing that service than with the cost of constructing or maintaining a comparable stretch of the Trans-Canada Highway in the determination of the value of that highway to any of the other nine provinces.
It is my contention-and I am sure it is shared by most reasonable Canadians-that the government of Canada has a serious moral and legal obligation to provide the people of Newfoundland with a modern and equitable transportation service. It has an obligation to ensure that the people in our province are not unduly penalized because we happen to be an island, as indeed we are at present. In 1949, when Canada and Newfoundland agreed to the terms of union, Newfoundland was separated by 90 miles of water from the mainland of Canada. Today we are still separated by the same 90 miles, and surely the Fathers of Confederation, the people who negotiated our terms, must have accepted at the time the proposition that by virtue of the fact that we were joining Canada and becoming a province of Canada, we should be treated equitably and equally with respect to transportation having regard to the 90 miles of water separating our province from the mainland.
I refuse to accept the proposition that it should cost a family of five or six travelling from Newfoundland to the Canadian mainland, or from the Canadian mainland to Newfoundland, any more than it would cost a family of the same size to travel the same distance between any other two provinces by way of surface transportation. If confederation is to be meaningful to our people and to, for example, the people of Prince Edward Island, I do not see why it should cost people travelling between the island provinces and the mainland any more than it would cost an upper Canadian to travel from Ottawa to Montreal by way of surface transportation.
The intent of my motion is to ask the government to consider the advisability of reducing the passenger car fare and freight rate structure to bring it in line with the cost of travelling to any other resident of any province of
Newfoundland Ferry Service
Canada over a stretch of 90 miles between his province and any other in this country. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has already admitted to the country that our transportation system is in a deplorable situation. Our only hope is that it does not become more chaotic and that the minister and his officials face up to the fact that CNR cannot be expected to become a profit-making, self-sustaining operation having regard to its present policy and the service that it is presently offering the travelling public of this country.
It is rather significant and timely that this motion should be debated in the House at this particular time, it being the twenty-fifth anniversary, the silver anniversary, of our becoming a part of Canada. Of course, as part of this celebration thousands of exNewfoundlanders and fellow Canadians will travel from cities in Canada to visit that newest province in the present year.
I think it is important that something be done as quickly as possible to bring in a rate structure for passenger cars and freight on these ferry services that will be comparable to the cost of travelling on any 90 miles of the Trans-Canada Highway. It is also important in that the economy of our province relies to a large extent on the tourist industry and its potential development. As a province that in many respects is unique and has managed to maintain its uniqueness, we have a tremendous tourist potential. By maintaining our individuality we can offer to the Canadian and American tourist something that cannot be found anywhere else on this continent.
Newfoundland can boast of being one of the oldest territories to be settled on the North American continent, and fragments of the early settlements are still in existence. We continue to enjoy a quality of life that has long been forgotten on this continent. We have managed to maintain the advantages of a quiet life, yet not primitive; of a happy people, yet not pretentious; of a scenery that is beautiful and natural, and not marred by industrial development.
In Newfoundland we recognize one very important point, and I have no hesitation in putting it forward here. It is that one day tourism will be our biggest and most profitable industry, provided of course the government recognizes that fact and is willing to co-operate with our province by formulating a more equitable policy with respect to our transportation needs. The progress we can achieve with respect to tourism will be determined to a large extent by the consideration and by the justice that we receive from the government of Canada.
I could go on for hours to talk about the high cost of living in the province, the high cost of shelter and the high cost of many other things attributed to a large extent to the high cost of transportation. But I am afraid there is nothing I could say that has not already been said in this chamber by colleagues over the past few years. In closing, Mr. Speaker, through you I suggest to the government that one of the most tangible efforts it could make, in its acknowledgement and appreciation of our twenty-fifth anniversary in confederation, would be to come up with a more equitable and more just transportation policy with respect to our province, and indeed with respect to the

Newfoundland Ferry Service
other Atlantic provinces as well. I am sure that one of my colleagues from P.E.I. will want to comment on ferry service with respect to his island province, so I will not encroach more on the time of the House except to request again, respectfully, that my motion be given serious and sympathetic consideration.
