speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that I have been categorized in the press as an old war-horse I can admit that I have heard many private member's motions and bills but I have never heard one that strikes me more as being possessed of sincerity, conciseness and thorough going reasonableness as that which has been presented by my colleague from St. John's West (Mr. Carter). He has been, since I have known him, a most diligent, thoughtful, persistent and persuasive representative of his people, and in my opinion he has spoken eloquently for them on a most, if not the most, important problem facing them on this very timely occasion of their silver jubilee as a part of this great dominion. It is a timely, thoughtful and most appealing subject and one which the authorities, at the moment vested with the governance of this country will neglect at their peril.
The hon. member was also correct when he said, about this province, as could have been said about mine a century ago, that in the days of our greater prosperity it was to our comparative advantage to be on and by the sea. In those days the Atlantic was a corridor of commerce. But now, as decade has followed decade, it has become disadvantageous for us to be in that once favoured location. We have seen the fulcrum of economic power move ever westward and, to use a polite word, we find ourselves on the unfortunate end of too many things such as transportation, price, the market, and so on. My hon. friend from Norfolk wants me to bring in a cow analogy; I would rather not do that because I want to retain the pristine purity of my remarks. But I have a fellow feeling for what the hon. gentleman has said. He has put his finger on the issue.
Why should the people of the two island provinces pay an exorbitant price to move to the other eight provinces of the dominion? Mr. Speaker, do you pay $9 to go from Manitoba to Saskatchewan? Is there a toll of $5 to cross a bridge here in Ottawa and go from Ontario to Quebec? Why, because God made us islands-and beautiful islands at that-should we have to pay every time we move to or from our island homes that are a part of confederation? It is a notorious injustice, and because we have had it so long is no reason why we should be expected to grow accustomed to it.
We live in an age when we talk about separatism in one part of the country and alienation in another, but because we in the Atlantic region have had our grievances for a century should not suggest that their very longevity detracts from their appeal, because certainly it does not. I think before any government of Canada can even conceive that it has made any kind of step to bringing about equality in this country it must make a major assault on the transportation inequities which face eastern Canada. For too long we have been out on the end. For too long we have paid dearly, partly not only in terms of remoteness from the major markets but also because of the very

matters which the hon. member for St. John's West has mentioned.
It was interesting that the hon. member mentioned the railway. The railway has diminished its function in his province and in mine, certainly, more than in any of the other provinces in the dominion. But when there is a rail strike, which two provinces suffer most because other means of road transportation cannot function? That is the irony we went through last summer in both our provinces. It caused cruel and shameful harm.
Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island have much in common. I was once intrigued by the suggestion of former premier Smallwood that he was not interested in maritime union at all, but he might think of union between P.E.I. and Newfoundland. I never was an advocate of maritime union because I have not been convinced of its advantages, but a union of Newfoundland and the Turks and Caicos Islands and other islands down in the Caribbean would give us a country that stretched from the Bahamas up to the top of Labrador, and that would appeal to me. It might give us some new dimensions, new visions, new perspectives and a new province too, but that is the kind of province I would like to see.
I notice that in the council of maritime premiers we have one of the fastest growing bureaucracies. I have been in Ottawa for 17 years so I know something about bureaucracies, but I think the council of maritime premiers is the largest empire without territory which the world has even seen, with the possible exception of the dying days of the Holy Roman Empire. Rather than considering questions of what we do organizationally and administratively to regroup and reconsolidate, we should apply ourselves in the way that my colleague has applied himself this afternoon, to a practical problem. I want to join him by supporting his contention that we must abolish this hardship upon the people of the island provinces. We must move away from the infliction upon them of a grievous toll as they move about this country. What was confederation all about, if it was not to provide a domain in which all citizens might move freely from one part to another?
The injustices outlined by the hon. member seem to me to indicate an infraction, an infringement and indeed a mockery of confederation. I will join him in not resting content until injustice is abolished and inequity corrected. I commend him for the vigour of his presentation and the authenticity of the argument he brought for a great province and a great cause, one which I support 100 per cent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my responsibility to participate in debate on the motion of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter). I believe, in all sincerity, that the spirit of festivity and joy that is characteristic of Newfoundlanders as they celebrate their twenty-fifth anniversary as members of confederation may very well account for the over-exuberance which gave rise to the motion before us. Certainly, were it not for the good will and amity that is prevailing between Newfoundland and the other nine provinces on this happy occasion, I would be tempted to term this motion as going a bit too far.

I am glad, and prepared, to address myself to the motion seeking reduced passenger car fares and freight rates on the North Sydney to Port aux Basques and Argentia route. On April 1, 1949, Canada undertook to provide a freight and passenger steamship service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, and Argentia was added in 1964. Since 1949 there have been only two marginal increases affecting passenger fares and freight rates, while revenue has dipped to less than 20 per cent of operating costs.
I believe that this motion would benefit from a closer examination of the facts. Mention was made of the Trans-Canada Highway. Annual operating costs in the order of $35 million, as opposed to freight and passenger revenue totalling little more than $7 million, do not to me constitute an exactly inequitable arrangement. And these figures, Mr. Speaker, do not reflect the sizeable capital investments made during the last quarter century. They total close to $220 million and are projected to rise even further over the next decade. With deficits far outstripping revenue and capital costs burgeoning, I find it difficult to comprehend the rationale behind the hon. member's motion.
I am one who, along with the federal government, strongly supports the concept of stronger ties and communications between Newfoundland and the mainland. Newfoundlanders have had to apply more careful planning and economic utilization of their resources in order to strive for a quality of life that compares favourably with the rest of Canada. It is much to their credit that-I am pleased to note-Newfoundlanders have succeeded to a stunning degree, in bending their environment and resources to their will. After all, who has not heard of the gigantic Churchill Falls hydro-electric project? Who is not aware of the massive iron ore operations at Wabush and elsewhere? Who does not know that the tremendous timber stands at eastern Labrador have enabled Corner Brook to produce newsprint that is sold on six continents? And, finally, what could be a more strategically apt and economically vital achievement than the development of an oil refinery 'at Come-By-Chance?
But, I must now return to the specific matter at hand. One has only to examine the Ministry of Transport's user-cost or beneficiary pay concept for it to become readily apparent that the ferry services from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland are run at great cost to the federal taxpayer and to the great benefit of its users. Newfoundland is the unquestioned beneficiary of this service. The user-pay concept of the Ministry of Transport does not apply nearly as severely as it does, for example, to air operators and travellers using ministry-owned facilities. The federal government does not intend to introduce a user-pay system which will finance all of its services in full. On the contrary, even now this concept is not applied universally across Canada. However, I do not think the federal government is being in the slightest bit unreasonable or insensitive to the needs of its people when it expects users to pay a reasonable share for the use of the extensive and valuable facilities and services provided. And in the case of the ferry services to Newfoundland, I do not think one can reach any other conclusion but that the user-pay concept is applied with kid gloves and tender loving care.
Newfoundland Ferry Service
I am not aware that the present passenger fare and freight rate structures pertaining to the Nova Scotia-New-foundland runs are acting as any sort of deterrent to the flow of goods and people along this route. On the contrary, my information indicates that the addition of vessels during peak periods coupled with plans for further supplements in the near future reflect the steadily growing use of this ferry service. Newfoundland, much to its credit, is increasing substantially in popularity with tourists who are spending more money and longer vacations there. This year, with the commemoration of its 25th birthday, promises to activate a tourist invasion of truly awesome proportions.
A 15 per cent annual growth in passenger-related vehicle movement should, to my mind, Mr. Speaker, raise the question of whether the ferry service capacity is sufficient rather than whether the time has arrived for the service to reduce fares and freight rates. I am sure the hon. member who proposed this motion is aware of the difficulties encountered in deploying vessels on a ferry service that carries 55 per cent of its passenger traffic during July and August. There is great expense involved in operating vessels at capacity levels of 10 per cent during the off season.
It would appear, once again, that the problems to be addressed by this House and my hon. friend would include the rationalization of vessel deployment to obtain maximum utility and maximum economy without sacrificing the quality of service for passengers. In addition, terminal capacity at North Sydney and Port aux Basques will shortly require expansion and, as I already mentioned, additional vessels are being planned for introduction to meet future passenger needs. All such improvements will involve large capital expenditures and I, for one, am in favour of upgrading this ferry service as the need arises. Such steps will further consolidate, both symbolically and tangibly, the historic links which have bound Newfoundland and the rest of Canada together on a steadily strengthening basis since 1949.
Turning to the movement of Gulf freight, this has been so heavy that rail car ferry charters have had to be extended and, if present growth rates continue, further ferry acquisitions and major shore facility extensions will have to take place for this service alone. In 1972, freight movement accounted for 78 per cent of the Gulf deficit at an average cost of $27 per ton to the federal taxpayer. This freight movement is, barring an upset in economic growth prognostications, likely to incur an even higher subsidization of goods by the taxpayer.
This situation does not strike me as being one calling for a reduction in freight rates. On the contrary. I would think that shippers are being provided with an economical conveyer of goods the like of which they would not have even if presented with the choice of competitive, free enterprise services. Private enterprise, the impetus that has made Canada forge ahead economically in such impressive fashion over the years, still forms the basis by which we stimulate growth and progress in this area. However, in the case of the ferry services in question, were it not for government intervention in providing a cheap, yet efficient, transportation service from Newfoundland to the mainland, the economic fortunes of our tenth province

April 8, 1974
Newfoundland Ferry Service
would not seem nearly as bright. Nevertheless, it would be foolhardy for me to suggest that all is well with our ferry services. Like all other operations, they suffer from inadequacies and imperfections.
The major problem, to which I alluded a few moments ago, lies in the allocation of ferry vessels where they will serve most effectively. Study and research with respect to improving the performance and seaworthiness of ferry vessels under all conditions is being conducted on a continuing basis. Service reliability under all conditions is another major consideration when planning the construction of new vessels, and the ultimate goal is to find a happy mean between an extravagant service and a hopelessly inadequate one.
With respect to the ferry service in Newfoundland, I do not imply it is an extravagant one. Far from it. It is the very lifeline which nurtures her relationship with the mainland and I would be rigidly opposed to any attempt to undermine or erode this vital connection. However, the question at issue today involves the reduction of passenger fares and freight rates. I do not believe such a move would benefit Newfoundland or its inhabitants to any significant degree.
With accelerating fuel, labour and maintenance costs, coupled with the need for heavy capital expenditures, it has been eminently generous of the federal government not to have passed on these added expenses to the users of the ferry service. Any proposed reduction simply does not make economic sense and belittles the appreciable contribution already made by the federal government in promoting economic expansion and tourist traffic to Newfoundland. This is another aspect we do not often talk about although it is related to the problem in question.
While disagreeing with the motion before this House today, I am equally in concord with Newfoundland's goals as a province. As I salute her past achievements, I wish her well in her future endeavours.

In describing user service the hon. member for St. Boniface used the words "tender loving care". This is analogous to the manner in which the

Department of Transport treats our province. The only thing tender loving care reminds me of is a hairspray. That is probably the way they are going to overcome our transportation difficulties.
The main problem in Newfoundland is isolation. This dictates that we must have special status in the consideration of our over-all transportation policy. One need only be reminded of the difficulties that we experienced last summer. This problem was alluded to by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie). Because of the CN strike, hundreds of thousands of tourists from the United States, indeed from all over North America, were stranded in Newfoundland for days, and sometimes weeks. This caused great incovenience to these people as well as to Newfoundlanders stranded on the Nova Scotia side because they could not get back to their families and their work. The situation reached almost emergency proportions. Fortunately, the strike was settled when it was, because it had reached the point where it was becoming an emergency from a medical and survival standpoint. This in itself should make the government realize that some form of communication must be ensured between these two provinces. I hope the government will soon realize this and begin to act. The government must support some kind of communication which would solidify both provinces.
Mention was made of the relationship between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and their relationship to the Trans-Canada Highway. The Trans-Canada Highway, which was built with such great fanfare by the federal government, was built on a deal to take away rail passenger service. However, even at this moment the Trans-Canada Highway is not up to standard. The government should realize its responsibility and take a look at the Trans-Canada Highway in Newfoundland. Millions of dollars need to be spent to provide proper passageway; there should be a proper road for the buses. The Trans-Canada Highway must be brought up to standard. As the hon. member for St. John's West stated, the Trans-Canada Highway must be considered a link between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and should be completed in our province. On April 22, hopefully my motion will be called. At that time I will elaborate on many other points of interest and concern to Newfoundlanders. We need a decent transportation policy and base in order to develop our many resources.
The hon. member for St. Boniface mentioned the cost to the government. I should like to remind him that the passenger rail service cost the federal government some $900,000. But immediately after that decision was taken, an order was issued by the Canadian Transport Commission to the effect that should the CN decide to abandon any other railway passenger services, it could be required to continue to operate them, in which case it would receive an 80 per cent subsidy. A few days ago I happened to come across the latest report issued by the CTC. It showed that subsidies amounting to $126 million were paid last year in respect of such passenger operations. And the figure will probably be higher in the years to come.
I should also like to remind hon. members that there is another isolated region only 10 or 11 miles from the north-
April 8, 1974

ern part of Newfoundland. Only that distance separates the island from the great mass of Labrador, whose inhabitants are completely isolated during the winter months and who have become familiar with living in conditions where they are shut off from goods and services. I hope the parliamentary secretary will remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) of my bill to establish a crossing between northern Newfoundland and Labrador. This would do wonders to encourage the development of the vast resources in that wonderful region.
In order that the motion may proceed to a vote, I end my remarks by expressing once again my support for the proposition advanced by my hon. friend from St. John's West.

Over the years they have established a high reputation not only for themselves but also for Newfoundland as a province.

It connects, on a year-round basis, one island, which is constantly populated, with the mainland and it serves a second island, or set of islands during the summertime when extensive use is made of them for recreational purposes. We are therefore familiar with the question of ferry boat routes and the cost of transporting people by water, though I admit the circumstances are totally different from those in respect of which the hon. member for St. John's West spoke this afternoon with great sincerity.
What I find surprising is this. Only two weeks ago the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Blenkarn), also a member of the Conservative Party, condemned the CN on a number of grounds. He said, as reported in Hansard at page 753:
One of the major problems the country faces is this: we are stuck with a national railroad which is improperly and ineptly managed. It is not managed as a business; it is managed in a political fashion, and therein lies the problem.

speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's West has made a good point. It is one which raises the question of the kind of policy we should follow in Canada in the field of public transportation. It is easy to make speeches about running a transportation company in a businesslike manner, but how is this to be done in a vast, thinly populated country such as ours without raising freight rates to a point at which only a limited section of the population could afford to pay them? Freight rates would need to be subsidized until the population was large enough to allow the subsidy to be discontinued. In the meantime, we need to consider something broader than the balance-sheet alone.
At the same time, the hon. member for St. John's West would be the first to press the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to see that the facilities and equipment of the vessels used on this type of service are not only modernized and kept up to date but are adequate to meet the needs of the public. This cannot be done by reducing tariffs and rates. A balance must be struck whereby some financial reserves are accumulated to improve facilities and equipment. Also, decent wages and salaries must be paid to the captains and crews of the vessels as well as the technicians employed in this kind of service, and must be similar to other salary levels in the country.
Reduced transportation rates will not bring this about. The only way to reduce rates without reducing revenue is through higher taxes, and then the question remains as to who is to pay these higher taxes. Perhaps the wish to keep the country together and to facilitate movement of people from one province to another is so strong that no one would object to this, but it sees to me it would at least be reasonable for any member requesting a reduction in rates to put the whole picture before the House and to discuss the consequences of such a measure. Then we would discuss the total scene, rather than just discuss the question of reducing rates in terms of accusing the government of total indifference.
However, I think the hon. member for St. John's West has made a good case in the sense that there is merit in providing a transportation service for all Canadians regardless of income, therefore permitting the exchange of

April 8, 1974
Newfoundland Ferry Service
individuals from one province to another. People living on an island are at a certain disadvantage as a result of geography. On the other hand, there are advantages to living on an island and they are not to be underestimated. The fact that a body of water has to be crossed usually tends to screen the island from visitors, and in this sense the island is not swamped by waves of thousands of tourists. I would not be at all surprised if the reason that Newfoundland has been able to retain its character and quality about which we hear and read so much these days is that it has been isolated from the mainland because it is an island. Probably the same concept applies to the beauty of P.E.I. Islands seem to be immune from industrial development and the pollution that arises therefrom because of the fact that they are removed from the mainstream of economic life.
I have tried, Mr. Speaker, in the very short time available to put forward a few thoughts. The motion of the hon. member for St. John's West raises a much broader question, one which was the subject of debate only ten days or two weeks ago on a motion introduced by the New Democratic Party. Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay) has assured us that the federal government is paying close attention to the Newfoundland ferry service to ensure that an uninterrupted and efficient service is maintained year round. As part of its ongoing program to upgrade and expand all ferry facilities on this service, Newfoundlanders in particular will be pleased to learn that a new rail car ferry costing about $14 million is scheduled for completion in late 1975. The vessel, a 7,000-plus ton twin-screw rail carrier capable of doing 17 knots, is designed to accommodate 34 rail cars on five tracks with stern loading.
Its secondary function is the carriage of highway trucks and trailers on containers between the terminals of Sydney and Port aux Basques. The vessel is, however, also suitable for certain other docks and sundry highway slips. The vessel, which will be capable of carrying rail cars weighing a total of 2,200 tons, is intended for year-round operation in the service across Cabot Strait and will be suitable in all respects for operation in the sea, wind, temperature and ice conditions encountered in that area.
A reliable and speedy gulf freight service is essential for the day-to-day exchange of vital commodities between Newfoundland and the mainland. The provision of yet another rail car ferry on this run is an example of the federal government's long-range planning and foresight in anticipating Newfoundland's present and future needs. I feel confident that with the addition of a new rail car ferry, coupled with the expansion of terminal facilities,

Newfoundlanders will be satisfied with the calibre of service and fairness of freight rates that characterize the transportation mode bearing the brunt of commerce between the island and Nova Scotia. I think we cannot help but be impressed by the manner in which this operation is managed by the federal government and by the dedication of the crews and shore personnel who labour year-round under harsh weather conditions to maintain this vital link that keeps Canada united and whole.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had come to my remarks on each part of this bill. Part I, dealing with exportation, would call for the return to the principle that it is always rather odd to speak of exporting natural resources such as petroleum when our country is forced to import it.
It would undoubtedly had been more logical and appropriate to adopt measures avoiding such a nonsensical situation where an oil exporting country finds itself at the mercy of foreign producers and has to suffer the repercussions of particular political events happening far from here, while we are oil producers ourselves.
However, this situation is the result of various circumstances and it should be corrected without delay.
Subject to the requirement that we should satisfy our particular needs inasmuch as it is physically possible, which should be done, it follows that when we are required to export, it is normal that we levy charges on our exports and at maximum prices. I think it is perfectly appropriate for our country to obtain the highest possible return on its natural resources when they are exported.
April 8, 1974

We agree on this principle of charges on each exported oil barrel, at the highest level.
With regards to Canadian oil prices restraint, we should ideally aim for price uniformity throughout Canada. But, as I already pointed out, the restriction imposed on transportation could result in quite tremendous cost differentials which could perhaps nullify that nice effort to ensure equality in prices across the country. If for each barrel of oil moved from one area of Canada to another the price turns out to be exorbitant that will result in people in some areas of this country having to pay an equally exorbitant price.
I think the minister and the government have not been specific enough on the line of action they would follow and it is only once we get that information that we will be able to judge whether oil is sold at an equal price in Canada. Price fixing based on foreign oil is as far as domestic consumption in Canada is concerned, somewhat arbitrary. Mr. Speaker, if we are fortunate enough to have natural resources as important as oil it seems to me that Canadians should really benefit from it, that is to say that for consumer needs the cost to the consumer should be in relation to how easy it is to obtain that product.
If in an entirely arbitrary way a price is fixed in relation to overseas I find that some details are missing in that respect and the line of reasoning followed lacks basis. I understand that that must have been related to the fact that we are also at the mercy of oil imports which would explain the price based on foreign oil but in principle if we get down to the root of the problem the fact still remains that we are faced with a situation where we can obtain a product at a given price but we are selling it back to the Canadian consumer at a much higher price simply because it also costs more abroad. I think that principle is wrong and I feel that that policy should have been based on an even lower price for the consumer of this country even if, as a consequence of that, we must increase the price of foreign-sold oil either through charges or otherwise, particularly since, Mr. Speaker, we are not sure whether the situation will always remain the same and that it will not be possible at a given time, for example, for eastern Canada, to buy oil at a lower price. How can one foresee that this bill might not handicap the commerce the Canadian consumer might benefit from, and the eastern consumer in particular?
So, to my mind, we should aim for the minimum price for Canadian consumers and the maximum price for foreign consumers at which to sell our oil according to international schedules. Mr. Speaker, when we come to Part III of this bill, which deals with additional domestic oil price restraint, we feel even more apprehensive because, through this additional control, federal authority in this regard could become absolute, and control in as important a field as that of oil could, at some point or other, deprive the provinces of the autonomy they have always cherished.
We therefore have reservations about an additional control at the hands of the federal government in this field. Moreover, in view of the extra controls this bill is designed to implement, wholesome competition is threat-
Petroleum Administration Act
ened. We wonder at times to what extent this control, these set prices will be depended upon, and to what extent profits will be neglected, as well as consideration of the fact that prices must be proportionate to production costs, to what extent due consideration will be given the fact that fixed prices are not much higher than production costs. Those dangers warrant mentioning.
Part IV, which deals with petroleum import cost compensation, is the one, Mr. Speaker, which to my mind contains the most contentious elements, for the simple reason that controlling the cost of foreign oil is most difficult to begin with. Just ask the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) when he had to buy heating oil what results he obtained and why he had to pay black market prices to avoid possible shortages.
It is therefore extremely difficult to achieve reasonable control over foreign oil prices, all the more so as a Canadian importer is faced with the fact that he is simply refunded the differential between the foreign oil price and the price set in Canada. We might be in a situation where the importer is not in the least interested in obtaining better prices or where at a given moment, he might be able to make profits.
In my opinion, this compensation for offshore oil price is not clear enough and may be dangerous, especially since certain details are not clear. For instance, subclause 51 (c) on page 21 states that will be considered as importers and entitled to compensation those importing petroleum into Canada to be purchased by other persons for the purpose of having it processed in Canada. If you read carefully this clause you may conclude that someday we will only have oil transiting through Canada to be processed here and exported abroad.
Controlling this will be an extremely difficult task and we wonder to what extent this control will be adequate. In brief, we would have preferred that the government did not have to introduce such a legislation. However, we understand the situation which existed and which is likely to exist again in the future and which could lead to many problems.
Therefore we understand the intentions, but we are afraid that the situation might get worse if we rely on those good intentions, since such pricing would not enable us anymore to think that we will be able at a given time to have a supply of heating oil at a very low price. We can no longer hope that the consumer will be able to get gasoline or other by-products of oil at a real low price.
That is why we are wondering whether this bill does not merely confirm the final victory of multinational oil companies, that will have won all along the line by causing prices to rise to the level they wished, in the case of a product that only comes from the soil after all and the real cost of production of which we are not so sure.
Considering the skyrocketing price paid by oil consumers during the last few months and the fact that on the other hand, the Quebec Minister of Finance says that seven oil companies have not paid a single cent in tax, we are asking ourselves questions. And in such circumstances, our fears are justified. That is why we suggest that the minister and the government should take into serious consideration every clause of this legislation so

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
that this measure will not be the ratification of the inflationary price rise of a Canadian product that the consumer could get at a much lower price and that we accept to sell at an exorbitant price.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if our foremost concern consisted in providing for the needs of the Canadian citizens instead of making profits, I am sure we would not be discussing now price rise and inflation in this regard but that we would think about something like this: We have oil, we are going to do everything in order that the Canadian consumer may at least buy it at the lowest price possible. I think this bill does not take that into account. On the contrary, it confirms a fact that results from world events that have nothing to do with us. With a good administration, Canada would never have known any oil crisis. Hence, it is arbitrary to determine prices; if there is a price increase, it is because of a lack of foresight and of adequate organization.
I am still deeply convinced that a country having ress-ources like oil can make it available to all citizens. So, if we decide arbitrarily on prices just to please oil companies, it is unfair to the Canadian consumer, and I think we should first consider essentially human factors in order to provide an adequate legislation.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer a few remarks on the bill before the House today I wish to make clear that the principle of the bill as expressed by the minister earlier is not in dispute. However, I feel bound to say that a clause by clause examination of the bill before us raises some questions with respect to the implementation process of the March 27 agreement, questions which I have no doubt will also be raised in the minds of provincial political leaders of the various provinces, and particularly the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
In preparing for this debate I reread the Prime Minister's statement delivered in the House of Commons last March 28, and I must state that the contrast between the tone of the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on that occasion and the tone and contents of Bill C-18 are startling, to say the least. I refer specifically to clause 36(1) of the bill before us which reads as follows:
Where no agreement is entered into pursuant to section 21 with the government of a producer-province, or any such agreement is terminated by the declaration of the parties, or, in the opinion of the governor in council, is not effective or is not capable of being effective, the governor in council may, by regulation, establish maximum prices for the various qualities and kinds of crude oil to which this part applies that are produced, extracted or recovered in that province (hereinafter in this part called the "exporting province").
Clause 36 of this bill is offensive in that it confronts our producing provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan once again with an ultimatum: either fall in line or we will legislate an agreement.
This bill goes far beyond the agreement and understanding reached between the first ministers on March 27 as explained by the Prime Minister. Under this legislation, the government seeks powers to establish oil prices within provinces under certain conditions. The March 27 agreement is to terminate in 15 months, yet this bill is open-

ended with respect to the term of its powers and provisions. Its penal provisions can only be described as draconian in their nature, and I refer you specifically to clauses 27 to 40 inclusive.
27.	A person who
(a) knowingly makes any false entry or statement in any record, book of account or other document required by this part or any regulations thereunder ...
is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year or both.
28.	(1) Every person who contravenes any of the provisions of sections 23 to 26 is guilty of an offence and is liable
(a) on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding twenty thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or both; or
(d) on conviction upon indictment, to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.
It is language of the sort contained in the clauses referred to which raises legitimate concerns in Canada's energy industry, concerns of the kind that could create for Canada energy shortages in the future where none now exist. Unless the government sheds its conspiracy theories and punitive mood it will damage not only the companies but the country. The whole federal government's performance dating back to last September in connection with energy matters raises substantial questions of competence, questions which can only give rise to profound uneasiness in the minds of all Canadians at the sweeping, far-reaching powers of control over the energy industry and the reduction in the provincial governments' ability to control the development and sales on a long-term basis of their natural resources.
Our Canadian energy industry which formerly exhibited strength and confidence is now wracked by uncertainties as to future government policy, uncertainty with respect to future prices, with respect to land leasing regulations, additional forms of taxation, and the formation of a national petroleum company and its possible role. These uncertainties and others constitute a major disincentive to Canada's petroleum industry and, if allowed to continue, will result in further loss of investor confidence which has already been badly shaken by recent events.
Under these circumstances, the ability of the industry to attract new venture capital to sustain Canadian resource exploration and development will be severely impaired and could even result in a flight of capital from Canada to areas offering a more stable economic environment, notably the United States.
Ultimately, of course, a long-term energy supply crisis could unnecessarily develop in Canada. Currently, Canada is in the very enviable position of producing more oil than it consumes. As a result of the national oil policy established in 1961, markets west of the Ottawa Valley have been reserved for western Canada crude, and western Canadian production in excess of domestic needs found an originally reluctant but now ready market in the United States. These markets, both domestic and in the United States* were a major factor in the development of the petroleum industry of western Canada and the level of domestic proven reserves we enjoy today.
However, Canada will become a net importer of oil at the end of this decade if new Canadian reserves are not

discovered and developed. Simplistically stated, Canada is at the stage in which the United States was in the mid 1960s in that we are already eating into the lead time required to discover, develop and bring new supplies to market.
In western Canada it probably takes five to seven years to do the necessary geological, geophysical and drilling work required to develop a specific producing area and start selling oil and gas. In the frontier areas the lead time is even longer. Gas was discovered at Sable Island in 1967 and some millions of dollars, 66 wells and six years later, the first gas is still a considerable period away from being produced and sold. Gas was found at Drake Point in the Arctic in July, 1969, and it is unlikely that any gas will be marketed from that area until the 1980s.
The long-term nature of such investment requires a careful evaluation of the political climate, favourable or unfavourable. The industry needs relatively stable political conditions and cannot operate satisfactorily on a stop and start basis. It is important to remember that it is only within the past 20 years that Canada has become a significant producer of crude oil. At the time of the Leduc discovery in 1947, Canadian production was no more than eight million barrels per year-about what we now consume in a week. It tends to be forgotten, in the light of recent events, that until very recently there was considered to be in North America an overabundance of natural gas.
Under these circumstances, natural gas prices in both Canada and the United States were kept distressingly low when compared with the cost of alternative, less attractive fuels. The direct result of this mistaken policy is the serious shortage of natural gas, particularly in the United States, prevalent today. For the balance of the 1970s it is estimated that the Canadian energy industry will require $30 billion of development capital. This new capital will have to be raised in competition with worldwide industry requirements, estimated at $500 billion during the same period.
The task of developing new energy resources deserves, and should be granted, the highest priority by the federal government and appropriate policies and regulations put in place to ensure that the necessary capital will be available and the necessary exploration and development work is carried on as expeditiously and rationally as possible. Piecemeal policies have no place in this context, and co-operation rather than confrontation is required. Other areas of the world are already competing for development dollars at this time and there is evidence that Canadian technical expertise and personnel are being lured away by more attractive offers in the United States and elsewhere.
The petroleum industry in Canada must be encouraged to press forward with the task of finding, developing, processing and bringing petroleum products to consumers. Policy-makers must provide a suitable operating environment within which the industry can perform its function. Parts of the bill before us are counterproductive in this respect and deserve review and revision by the minister proposing their passage.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-18 puts into effect the agreement reached, after many weeks and months of negotiation, between the federal government and the provinces and establishes many important precedents in Canada. It establishes one oil price right across the country. It establishes a two-price system for Canadian oil, namely, a domestic price that is much lower than the international price and it also maintains the export tax on Canadian oil sold to the United States. It further recognizes the fact that oil and the other natural resources of this country come under provincial jurisdiction and law. That is a most important fact which all of us must recognize in a debate of this sort.
There are a couple of things that concern me as a member who comes from one of the oil producing provinces, Saskatchewan, as I look at this bill and rise to participate in debate on it. The first thing I notice is that the agreement reached between the consuming and producing provinces will give the people of Saskatchewan actually less per barrel of oil than they were receiving under the voluntary agreement which expired in March. They will now receive $6.50 per barrel under this agreement which we are now legislating, but under the voluntary arrangement they were receiving $6.60 per barrel, made up of an outright sum of $5 per barrel for oil sold in the province, plus 50 per cent of the export tax, which on the production of oil in Saskatchewan worked out at about $1.60 per barrel, making a total of $6.60. So as a result of the agreement reached in Ottawa, the actual direct revenue to the people of Saskatchewan will be a lesser sum of money than they were receiving before those negotiations concluded.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, as a member from a producing province I am also concerned that the producing provinces are not getting a share of the export tax. Our party made it clear right from the outset, through the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) and through our leader, that the producing provinces deserved a share of the export tax. It seems to me particularly unfair that the export tax should be used to subsidize the consumers in eastern Ontario, the four Atlantic provinces and Quebec, because when this is done it is using funds that should at least in part go to the producing provinces.
What I am really saying is that I agree with the fact that we are subsidizing the eastern market because of the international situation, but I am arguing that the subsidy should be paid on the basis of equality and equity right across the country, without being taken solely from the revenues due the two producing provinces. An appropriate analogy might be if we were to lower the price of automobiles in Canada and if we were to accomplish this by subsidizing buyers with money taken from Ontario because that is where the automobiles are produced, or if we were to do the same kind of thing with farm machinery and take the subsidy from Ontario provincial resources because that is where it is produced.
It seems to me that this is all part of the built-in tradition that goes against equity in this country in terms of distribution of wealth and income. And if it were not for certain other developments I would have a difficult time being convinced that this is the right direction in which to proceed. However, it is my understanding that in

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
the case of Saskatchewan the federal government is willing to look at some significant trade-offs, or what might be called quid pro quo, with respect to things that would lead to greater industrialization of our province, such as a major steel industry.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has suggested that we should take a look at the freight rate system and correct some of the inequities in it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is talking about stabilizing the income of farmers in Saskatchewan, and indeed of farmers all over Canada. If some of these things are coming, then perhaps the deal that is before us from the point of view of my province will be good, that is, if we have these particular trade-offs. If our oil is sold across the country at lower than world prices, that will be all right with us if we can purchase other commodities coming into our province at lower than the world price, and if our oil is used to help build an industrial base in Saskatchewan giving us equality with other parts of Canada. That is a very important factor in this debate and one that should be recognized by all members regardless of the regions they represent.
I suggest that the province of Saskatchewan is a totally different case from the province of Alberta. In effect, here we are dealing with apples and oranges, with two radically different situations. Saskatchewan is basically a have-not province and Alberta is a have province. Alberta has vast quantities of oil, not only in conventional sources but in the tar sands. Saskatchewan has only about 80 million to 85 million barrels trapped under its land and will run out of oil in nine to ten years. That is something that must be clearly understood when we are talking about this bill. Saskatchewan is essentially an agricultural province, and if we do not expand our industrial base, after the oil has gone what will we have left?
At present we have 4 per cent of the nation's population, and our provincial population has been falling for a number of years. In 1968, Saskatchewan had 962,000 people; in 1973, it had only 906,000-a drastic drop. If the same proportionate drop took place in Ontario over the same period, it now would have a population of six million instead of eight million. In effect, it would eliminate the city of Toronto. Just imagine the effect that would have on Ontario. The same thing applies to provincial income. We depend so much on the agricultural industry and on funds derived from natural resources. In Saskatchewan the fluctuation of income can be as great as 40 per cent from one year to another. Compare that with Ontario, or with the nation as a whole, where income fluctuation has never been over 10 per cent from one year to another.
Why does this happen in Saskatchewan? There is a very obvious reason. The rural parts of the country, and Saskatchewan is perhaps the most rural of all, do not have an integrated economy. They do not have an industrialized, developed economy. This is because of the old national policies which we have pursued for so many years, directed developing the industrial parts of the country, particularly the golden horseshoe in southern Ontario.
These have been policies that have been based on tariffs and on a railway system designed to take raw materials from the hinterland to the industrial heartland. As a result, we find an area like Saskatchewan is supplying new materials and foodstuffs in an unprocessed state to

factories in eastern Ontario, or indeed to places like Vancouver, where the raw materials are processed and manufactured and where, of course, there are the jobs that go with the processing and manufacturing.
Commodities and items such as livestock, rapeseed and natural mineral resources are shipped from the prairies at a rate lower than the equivalent weight of finished goods. There is therefore an incentive to ship goods from the prairies, and thus an incentive to export jobs as well, which means that the people leave the rural areas. All this will have to change, and a start could be made with the oil policy in this country which could expand into a new national policy, one that would treat all commodities the same and remove inequities in the freight rates system and develop the economy in a rational way. There should be equity of conditions. That could be done if we set our minds to it.
This bill concerns me on other grounds as well, and I hope this House will look at them. One concern is that under the bill, multinational oil companies will have another windfall or another rip-off in terms of profits. We all know the figures for the last year and we all know that the oil companies are going to be big winners. In Alberta the provincial government has decided to split the extra revenue 65 per cent for the province and 35 per cent for the oil companies. This means that the $2.50 will be split 88 cents for the oil companies and $1.62 for the people of Alberta, giving the oil companies in the province additional revenue of some $528 million per year. Actually, it will probably be higher because of some additional things that have developed during the last few days. This is of great concern to me and I think we should look at this part of the bill.
Another thing that concerns me is the way the government is going to subsidize the oil companies in eastern Ontario, Quebec and the four Atlantic provinces. They will subsidize them, trusting their accounting system and their judgment on how much the oil is going to cost when they purchase it offshore. I suggest we are going about this the wrong way. We should, instead, establish a national petroleum corporation or marketing board that would purchase all offshore oil and sell it to the people in the east. That would be easier and less bureaucratic than the system we are getting into.
How do we know how much Exxon is going to pay for oil in Abu Dhabi, Saudi Arabia or some other states in the Middle East? How do we know how much of the price paid for oil in Canada is real and how much artificial? How much of it will be theirs, because they are handling it with other subsidiaries? How much can they obtain, because it is in the hands of parent companies in the United States? How much information can we really get? Mr. Speaker, these are questions that I ask and that our party wants answered before the bill passes.
I also wonder about the fact that the bill is to be administered by an allocation board. Why is that? When the allocation act passed it was my understanding that the only time this board would be operational, except for a small staff, would be if the government or parliament declared an energy emergency. Why will this legislation

not be administered by the National Energy Board or the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, instead of building another bureaucracy to do it? These are a few of the questions that I ask, Mr. Speaker, a few of the questions that I want answered and which I believe that the people of Canada want answered before we pass this legislation.
Clause 54 of the bill, on page 24, deals with special cases. An importer may ask for more funds than are provided under the bill if he meets irregular or abnormal circumstances. I wonder how that provision will be interpreted and whether it might not open the door to companies to make higher profits. I have serious questions about that part of the legislation.
As we debate this bill I think we should see it as a step toward a new national policy in this country. I do not know why we do not have two-price systems in other commodities. As a Saskatchewanite, I sometimes wonder why it is that two of the three commodities for which we have a two-price system are produced in Saskatchewan- oil and wheat. We do not have a two-price system for commodities such as iron, lumber and nickel. It seems to me that we should have a two-price system for them and charge a lower domestic price than the world price. We should have an export tax, for example, on commodities and channel the funds back to the provinces and Ottawa for further development of the resources and basic commodities of the country. We should be pursuing such a policy. This would help fight inflation and help the economy. I do not know why we are not doing it. I suggest we should be moving in this direction.
Mr. Speaker, when we discuss gas and oil we should be considering public ownership. We should be treating these as public utilities, owned and controlled by the people as hydroelectricity is in most parts of the country. We should examine the example of Saskatchewan where all the money gained from oil is going back for exploration and development of the gas and oil industry in the province, under public ownership and control. That should be done at the national level, with agreements between the provinces and the federal government.
When I hear the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) speak about the development of the tar sands, I am terrified. He has been going around the country talking about bringing in billions of dollars of capital from Japan, Europe and the United States, developing the tar sands and using the revenue from the sale of oil to repay the debts accumulated in building tar sands plants. Who is calling the shots here, Mr. Speaker? That plan was devised by Herman Kahn at the Hudson Institute. It strikes me as strange that the Minister of Supply and Services would be peddling Herman Kahn's ideas. It strikes me as strange that he should have made representations to cabinet on two occasions last fall about the development of the tar sands.
It strikes me as strange, Mr. Speaker, because I suggest there are certain connections between the Hudson Institute and the Liberal Party. The Hudson Institute has opened an office in Montreal, Hudson Institute (Canada), which is headed by one, Claude Frenette. He is no stranger to the Liberal Party. He is very close to certain cabinet ministers, such as the Minister of Supply and Services. He
Petroleum Administration Act
was also a vice-president of Power Corporation. I wonder about his connection with Power Corporation and the talk about Power Corporation going into the oil business.
These are questions that I throw out. Who is calling the shots? Who is advising on a national oil policy for Canada and a national resources policy? Is it actually the government of this country, or is it the multinational corporations or some of the big business concerns in this country and abroad? Mr. Speaker, these are a few of the questions that I raise about the bill before us, and I think they should be answered before the legislation passes this House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate almost with a sigh of relief, relief that the question of crude oil pricing in Canada is finally approaching the point of solution. We in the House of Commons, and indeed all Canadians, will be able to get back to what are more important questions over the long run, namely, taking advantage of the tremendous opportunity Canada has with regard to energy. I say "almost a sigh of relief" because it would have been a genuine sigh of relief had the minister and this government restricted themselves to bringing in a bill which had the purpose of implementing and giving legislative back-up to the agreement reached between the first ministers at the long lunch at 24 Sussex Drive.
It is a relief for me, this House of Commons and, I am sure, all Canadians to hopefully be seeing the end of an incredible history of vacillating policy commitments, contradictions and inconsistencies. Commitments were made one day and broken the next. This goes back over a considerable length of time. Indeed, two years ago the minister first promised he would be generating an energy policy that would be coming out that winter.
The question of pricing in particular became an issue on September 4 last. We left for the summer recess in July, only to be called back in August because of a railway strike. While we were on recess, the leader of the New Democratic Party was travelling around the country saying that he had just about had it with this government and he did not know how much longer he could support them. I notice he has been saying the same thing during the past couple of days.
We came back to this House and legislated the railroaders back to work. The government felt compelled to make some statement on inflation. The cost of living was going up at that time at what we thought was an astronomical rate of 8 per cent. We know now that was almost low compared to what the government managed to achieve this year. In any event, the government felt compelled to make a statement. The cabinet met through Labour Day weekend. On September 4, at 2 p.m., we came into the House to hear a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). We had to adjourn for two hours because the statement had not yet been typed.
We came back to the House two hours later and were informed there was a freeze on the price of western Canadian crude oil. As a sop, if you like, to western Canada, the province of Alberta in particular, the government also said it was going to build a pipeline to Montreal

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
in accordance with the wishes that had been expressed over the previous eight or nine years. It was nine days later that the government realized it could not make this freeze work, as a result of section 83 of the National Energy Board Act which required the National Energy Board to restrict any exports of Canadian crude oil at less than market value.
The government then quickly invented an export tax and put it in place. At that time it was 40 cents. That was on September 13. This gave rise to all of the history with which we are now only too familiar, the understandable cries of concern from the producing provinces and a great deal of concern by those on this side of the House about the direction the government was taking. There was then the Middle East war, the Arab embargo, all the resulting moves by OPEC nations, and so on. No one could have foreseen this. Whether the OPEC nations took advantage of a situation, or only obtained their just due, I think there can be arguments on both sides.
What is appalling, totally unacceptable and disgusting is the claim by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and this government that this price freeze and the export tax was a demonstration of their tremendous foresight and, indeed, without this export tax and price freeze they would have been unable to implement the pricing policy that appears in this bill. That is a bunch of nonsense. That move on their part caused nothing but ill-will. It will take a great number of years before that is cleansed from our society. Regrettably I make that statement.
I have no interest in maintaining the animosity which might exist between certain people in western Canada and eastern Canada. It is very unfortunate for this nation that it exists, but if there is fault it should not be placed with the manufacturers or the displayers of bumper stickers. It should be placed where it belongs, with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
I will cite a further example, if any further proof is needed of this government's deceitfulness. Although the government claims it had a tremendous amount of foresight in its moves of September 4 and 13, we need only look at the Toronto Star which,was quoted this afternoon by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). The Prime Minister is quoted as saying he did not feel the federal government had any right to interfere in the energy pricing policy. In terms of an oil pipeline to Montreal, we need not look any further than page 14 of the energy analysis which the government tabled at the end of June last, in which it is stated:
To date, the security threat has not appeared serious enough to justify the very costly arrangements of supplying the region east of the Ottawa Valley with western Canadian crude oil.
It is a sad history of inconsistencies, broken promises, vacillations and incompetence. I could think of a few other words but they might not be parliamentary. As the Middle East war produced its supposed embargo and actions by the OPEC nations, we saw really incredible behaviour by this government. They behaved very much like the character in a children's story about the sky falling in. I think the name of the character is Chicken-licken who said, "The sky is falling in, the sky is falling in." The government were literally running around in circles saying, "The

sky is falling in." They said, "We won't have any oil this year. We will be short of oil. People will freeze in the dark." The Turkey-lurkeys said, "Yes, indeed the sky is falling in. We had better do something." In the case of the children's story, it was Chicken-licken, Foxy-loxy and Turkey-lurkey. Indeed, it was Foxy-loxy who convinced them the sky was falling in in the first place.
Foxy-loxy in this case is the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who, for his own purposes, convinced some people that indeed we were in a terribly perilous situation with regard to energy, we would have terrible shortfalls and we must act to implement everything he suggested. Unfortunately, Chicken-licken and Turkey-lurkey were not eaten, as they were in the story. I suggest that is only right, because poor Foxy-loxy would have had indigestion.
It cost the people of Canada at least $15 million because of some asinine heating oil purchases by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). The story unfolded as the result of persistent questioning from this side of the House. In terms of the government's purchase of heating oil last winter, it is absolutely unbelievable. They paid an average of 79 cents per gallon for heating oil which is now being offered for sale at 25 cents a gallon in Montreal, and there are no takers. It is incredible. Indeed, the amount of money that that oil deal cost was far in excess of the cost of the Bonaventure. In terms of the Bonaventure, we at least had the Auditor General look into it. It is about time the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) asked the Auditor General to look into this heating purchase, because there are still many unanswered questions. Another incredible aspect of this story was illustrated on December 6 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was making his statement indicating that the freeze would not end on January 31. Incidentally, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources had promised just the night before that it would. Nevertheless, the Prime Minister used this opportunity to expound upon all of the new national oil policy initiatives the government was taking, among which was a decision to establish a national petroleum company. The Prime Minister said, and I quote from Hansard:
Finally, the company will assist in assuring reliable and adequate imports of oil to meet present and foreseeable new needs for foreign oil.
The government has found in recent weeks that it can play an important role in purchasing petroleum and petroleum products. It proposes to exercise this role through the company.
Well, if it is the wish, and if it is the will, and if the Chicken-lickens and the Turkey-lurkeys Liberals and NDPs force a national petroleum company on this unfortunate country, at least let us hope that those individuals who were working for Supply and Services in connection with this heating oil purchase are not hired by the company to act as its agents. Because if we lose $15 million every time the company makes a purchase in the market we will soon find it is costing us a very substantial percentage of the federal tax revenue.
During this period, during this frantic "the sky is falling in period," when everybody, or at least everybody on the Liberal side and in the NDP corner of the House, was convinced that disaster had struck, the Minister of
April 8, 1974

Energy, Mines and Resources used the crisis atmosphere first to get cabinet approval of his national petroleum company, second to expand the responsibilities of his department and agencies accountable to his department, and third to introduce the energy supplies emergency bill and get it through the House.
In that situation this party made every possible effort to determine the facts in terms of Canada's shortfall in energy reserves this winter. We made every possible effort to see that expert witnesses were brought before the committee in order truly to determine Canada's position. At every step our moves were obstructed by the government and by the NDP. They said, "How could you be so irresponsible? Don't you know there is going to be a tremendous oil shortage this winter? If you are going to be responsible, pass this act immediately so that the government can set up its emergency energy allocation board and allocate the available supplies."
Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say that indeed we did back down from some of these demands and we did give approval to the bill, with some important changes. We did manage to get a degree of parliamentary control, but with the passage of that bill one of its provisions was the creation of another empire for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Ressources to administer, namely, the energy allocation board. This energy allocation board was supposed, according to that bill, to be responsible for implementing and allocating energy supplies within the country should we be faced with a situation of shortage. Indeed, we were faced with a shortage, and its most knowledgeable people stated there was no reason for us ever to be faced with a shortage since we were self-sufficient and all that was needed was a reasonable amount of good planning. This board really did not have a job. I see that as a result of part III of this bill the energy allocation board now has a job. I suppose I am happy to see it; I hate to see underemployed civil servants.
Mr. Speaker, I have omitted a considerable amount of detail in this sad story of the government's performance in the energy sector over this last year and a half, actually since the last election. It truly is a sad story and I sincerely hope, for the benefit of all Canadians, that the bill marks the end of that sort of behaviour; that from now on we shall see responsible, consistent behaviour from whoever is minister of energy, mines and resources and it will be in accordance with the type of advice which is offered in this book. It is incredible to me that the government would offer this energy analysis for consideration at the end of June last year, a booklet which contained so much excellent advice, and then proceed totally to ignore it and to confuse, distort and disrupt the situation to an unbelievable extent.
In particular, I wonder why the minister will not, in spite of our representations, follow his own advice, namely, that given on page 9 of this energy analysis that no national policy can be contemplated without the fullest intergovernmental consultation and consensus. That is excellent advice, yet we have an admission from the minister that this bill, implementing a very important agreement in terms of price, has never been submitted to the provinces; that the provinces have never been asked to respond. The minister told us this is an important part of
Petroleum Administration Act
national energy policy. He stated today that there has to be the fullest consultation between governments before a national oil policy can be implemented, and it puzzles me that the minister will not take his own advice.
Parts I and IV of the bill implement the agreement reached between the first ministers at their luncheon recently and we have no general disagreement with this aspect of the bill. Part I provides for the export tax, legalizing the tax which has been in existence since September 13. We think it is about time it was legalized. Part IV provides a subsidy so that Canadians east of the Ottawa Valley will pay the same price for petroleum products as those in the area west of the Ottawa Valley. This has been the policy of the Conservative Party, one price across Canada, since well before the government even thought of it, so we can hardly object to that provision.
However, we do object to some of the aspects of part IV because it seems as though the government has looked at four or five different ways of doing things and has chosen the most difficult and the most complicated to administer. As to parts II and III, let me say that if we seek a uniform price less than the world market price, all that is required is an export tax. A uniform price existed in Canada prior to any export tax at all. It was based roughly on the Chicago price as being the main market area, and that was pretty well uniform all over Canada served by western Canadian crude. It is clear that if you put an export tax on crude destined for the Chicago market, it will lower the price of western Canadian crude. The same conditions which resulted in uniformity of price before will still apply and we would have a uniform price system. That is all that is necessary.
In part II of the bill the government has gone far beyond this. It is proposing a complicated set of regulations in clauses 22 and 23. Why it has taken this route and imposed this unnecessary complication raises very serious questions in my mind. Quite frankly, I can be forgiven if I suggest that perhaps this provision is directed at the provincial marketing boards. It may be there is another motive behind this move by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Rather than seeking to achieve uniform price as he claims, perhaps he is seeking to outlaw or to disqualify the operations of any provincial marketing boards that exist in Saskatchewan and Alberta. If that is the case, I think this is a very devious way of going about it. It may be a valid thing to do, but surely if the government is going to stick to its commitment to consult, this step should be taken after consultation and with the consent of the provinces, not as a result of a unilateral proposal that is snuck into a bill in which it does not belong.
These kind of ad hoc addenda to legislation to achieve some other purpose are becoming a habit with this government, not a habit which we should condone. Certainly this party will want to have a good look at this particular aspect. We are not going to be bullied into passing these parts of the bill in the same way as we were bullied into passing the energy supplies emergency bill last Christmas. The fact of the matter is that the sky is not falling in and we do have time to consider, to consult, to call witnesses

and to make sure that we pass good legislation. This is our responsibility to the people of Canada.
As for part III, this section of the bill raises very great concerns. It appears to be, to all intents and purposes, a club to hold over the producing provinces so the federal government can say, "Unless you reach agreement with us, we shall impose our agreement. Furthermore, we shall impose it without consultation and without the approval of parliament; we will do it on the word of the minister alone". As my colleague for Peace River stated this afternoon, this is a part of the bill that we cannot swallow. As my colleague also indicated, before we can take the word of the minister as to a commitment, we want to make sure it is given under oath.
Clause 34, which provides that part III shall come into force on a day to be fixed by proclamation, should be amended. The act should come into force only after approval by the House of Commons. Then we will have had an opportunity to be sure that the proper consultation between the federal government and the provinces has occurred. We would then know that if an agreement had been reached it was not because the minister or the federal government in general had used this club to which I have referred.
Part III is very similar to the other parts in that it contains a great deal of detail and unnecessary law in terms of implementing a uniform price across Canada. We do not feel that this is the desirable way of approaching the matter. It is quite unnecessary to be so complicated. We suspect the minister has other motives in mind.
Part IV of the bill implements the program to subsidize imported oil coming into eastern Canada, so that the price Canadians in that part of Canada pay for their oil is the same as the price Canadians in other parts of Canada pay. As I have indicated, it is obvious that the government has selected the most complicated subsidy program imaginable. The government is going to subsidize on a separate basis literally every single boatload of oil imported into Canada. The government must have chosen to do things in this way because the energy allocation board has built up such a staff that it needs a complicated method like this to keep the staff busy; I can think of no other reason.
Surely if we can have one uniform export tax we can have one uniform import subsidy; the same basic principles apply and it would be much easier to implement. Customs and excise officials could keep track of the amount of oil imported, and companies could apply for their subsidy in the same way as they pay their import duties. Administration would be dramatically simplified and the powers that the government asks for in part V would not be necessary. Therefore, I seriously question why the government has taken this unnecessarily complicated way of subsidizing the importation of crude oil into the region east of the Ottawa Valley.
There is also no provision in the bill to cover the situation we witnessed this winter where Canadian crude was shipped from the port of Vancouver through the Panama Canal to the eastern part of the country, thus decreasing our reliance on Middle Eastern crude which was under embargo, and possibly helping us avoid a shortfall this winter. Under the proposed subsidy program it would be impossible for a company to do this again, because clearly

it would have to pay all the transportation costs out of its own pocket. The company would be better off bidding for some of the high-priced Middle East oil at $30 or $40 a barrel. It would not matter how much it bid for it, because it would get a subsidy from the Canadian government.
This brings me finally to why I contend the subsidization program is wrong in principle. It gives companies no incentive to shop around. As I say, it does not matter what they pay for oil, because they are going to get a subsidy. If a company has an option on some oil, then regardless whether the oil is $40 a barrel or $50 a barrel, the government will pay a subsidy which will bring the price down to $6.50 a barrel. Therefore, I contend the program is wrong and should be thoroughly examined.
To me, part V is the most incredible part of the bill. The powers granted to enter premises and seize records and information go beyond the bounds of common decency. I know we tend to worry about the privacy of the individual and not about the privacy of corporations, agencies and so on, but I think it is about time we did give them a little consideration. Yet under this legislation the federal government could walk into the premises of the Energy Resources Conservation Board of Alberta and seize all their records. They could walk into the premises of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in the province of Saskatchewan and seize all their records. I contend it is absurd to give the federal government this sort of power.
