subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with this bill we are being asked to give parliamentary approval to a major decision, I think one of the most major decisions that has been taken in the life of this country and one that could well set a pattern for the future of the nation. I think the best that can be said is that it is a solution, but it certainly poses the significant question: Is it the best solution at the moment, and what will it lead us to?
It is significant, it seems to me, in that it confiscates the natural resources of some provinces for a time, to be used in the so-called national interest. This is something that rarely has been done in our country, but there have been occasions in the past. There have been occasions during which prices paid to producers for very valuable commodities have been deliberately made significantly lower than the market value. One such occasion was in respect of the price of wheat during the Second World War when Canada sold wheat to our allies at prices far below world prices. Memories of this action in respect of wheat are particularly vivid among the western agricultural community, and there is no doubt that considerable western alienation or skepticism about central Canada arose as a result of the pricing of that wheat so low on the markets of the world.
By adopting a mechanism for pricing crude oil in Canada at prices much below the world level, which might seem like a very good idea for the moment, we may well be
Petroleum Administration Act
opening a Pandora's box of trouble in the long run by exposing our trade in the markets of the world to considerable retaliatory action. No one will dispute the fact that a sudden rise in the price of crude oil could create great hardships to home owners and other users of our oil, and this is of particular importance in view of the cold Canadian winters. A cushioning mechanism is needed to avoid undue exploitation and hardship, and fortunately we are able to do this because of the situation. It is no secret that other forms of energy, even those controlled by government agencies, are to increase in cost rapidly within the next few years. Mr. Schreyer, Premier of Manitoba, has announced that Manitoba Hydro will experience a 14 per cent increase over the next three years, bringing the increase to well over 50 per cent. At the present time Manitoba enjoys one of the lowest hydro rates in Canada, indeed on this continent.
Just a year ago, at the time of the Manitoba election compaign, the premier accused some members of the opposition of misrepresenting the cost of hydro development in that province when they suggested it would require $171 million in respect of the so-called Winnipeg control, yet now the chairman of Manitoba Hydro has said the same thing will be worth $233 million. The same thing is true in respect of the Nelson River project. The cost of installation was said to be $1 billion, but the latest estimates are in the neighbourhood of $4 billion. Just as with private corporations, government corporations are finding it impossible to hold the price line.
By reaching in and setting the price of products, the federal government has effectively taken away from the provinces the control of their own natural resources. By setting a two-price system we are inviting the same thing to occur in respect of other commodities as that which occurred in respect of wheat; and this has already occurred to some extent with lumber, pulpwoood, plywood, paper, products of the auto industry and many other products controlled by government.
I suggest that we have been perhaps unduly concerned about oil because it has been so cheap that we have come to rely on it in the western world perhaps to an abnormal extent. I suggest that control of oil prices would not have come about except that the producing provinces happen to be in western Canada. Had oil producers been in Ontario and Quebec it is obvious that a much different approach would have been taken to the problem. Oil prices would in all likelihood have been allowed to increase, with perhaps a subsidy to help those unduly affected.
So far as confederation is concerned, the westerner believes that to a certain extent his resources are being used for the good of Canada generally without any equivalent care being taken to compensate him for this. We can expect to see increasing disregard for provincial rights by this government as time goes on. Enormous bureaucratic control will have to be employed in order to exercise jurisdiction over this commodity. This will certainly decrease private initiative and investment in respect of oil activity in the oilfields.
The way the so-called $6.50 a barrel was arrived at is interesting. The ten provincial premiers and the Prime

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
Minister (Mr. Trudeau) sat down and decided what a barrel of oil should cost. Why is the same thing not done in respect of the price of eggs, beef or other commodities? It is obvious that not much thought was given to the continuation of supplies of oil, oil exploration and the oil industry. It is difficult to see how exploration can continue with the price of oil at $4 a barrel while it is necessary to compete for exploration money with other parts of the world where the price of oil is much greater.
Even if we say the government can enter the exploration field, this requires dollars which then would not be available for other purposes. This method of dealing with the problem leaves much to be desired. It seems logical that if the price at the wellhead is to be increased, the money could go to the oil companies directly and that the tax structure, including an excess profits tax if necessary, should be employed to make sure that undue profiteering will not take place. In this way legitimate exploration and development would be rewarded.
What has happened is that the three provinces, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan can add an extra $1.7 billion revenue from their producing wells. Some of this money may be allocated to the oil companies to encourage them to increase their exploration and developmental activity. However, there is no compulsion on them to do so. Saskatchewan apparently intends to give nothing, and presumably intends to carry on its own exploration. It seems at this time that the plans of the provinces are hazy. It is almost certain that most of the revenue accruing to these two provinces will have to be used in the service industries to service the people in the normal way.
At the same time, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will receive large sums of money and tax equalization grants from Ottawa while being insulated against realistic prices of oil. It has been calculated that over $100 million of additional equalization payments will be forthcoming from Ottawa and that most of it will go to Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. In respect of the provinces which list their new-found wells in their capital accounts, this will mean that they will not be calculated as part of Ottawa's national tax equalization formula.
The end result is that Manitoba and Ontario will pay extra for oil but will receive no offsetting compensation from Ottawa. Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan will receive tremendous windfalls, although their motorists will have to pay extra for gasoline. Quebec and the Alberta region, although having to pay extra for gasoline, will receive handsome equalization payments from Ottawa. So Ontario and Manitoba will not benefit to the same extent. Some people might ask why Ontario needs this benefit since it is so rich in any event.
In relation to the export tax and our trading stance with the rest of the world, there are some very interesting developments. We can almost certainly expect retaliation for our actions. I would think this export tax would be considered by the rest of our trading partners as a nontariff barrier. We will not be able to protest if extra tariffs should be placed on bauxite, orange juice and many other tropical items we are unable to produce in our country.
This whole bill, although relatively simple, brings forward some interesting discussion about Canada's role, particularly as a trading nation. We are a trading nation.

We have always relied to a great extent on the export of energy to help our foreign exchange position. We have imported low-cost oil in eastern Canada and we have imported coal into Ontario. At the same time, we have exported surplus energy to the United States midwest. We have exported electricity at a variety of border locations in Manitoba. For instance, Manitoba has a very good arrangement with its United States counterpart. It exports electricity during the summer in order to keep the Americans cool during their hot weather period, while during the winter the electricity is retained for the heating of homes. I think this is a very good arrangement.
One might ask what would happen if the United States decided not to export coal to Canada? In certain circumstances they would certainly be justified in doing so, and this would create many problems for our country. The world's low-cost energy has been held in the hands of a few nations. We must decide whether we want to concentrate on our own security or maintain our position as a trading area. It seems that for many years we pressured the United States to allow us to export oil, yet now many Canadians are saying we should not do this. One could hardly blame the United States for attaching little validity to what we said many years ago.
We should not disrupt international trade agreements so long as we do not endanger our current security. It has been recognized that trade in energy is only part of our total trading pattern but that any withdrawal from this area would create many problems for us. Another important area about which we must think is the way in which we use our energy resources and whether or not we develop them for our own purposes. There are conservationists who say that we should not develop any energy sources because this leads to pollution, and so on. Unfortunately, however, no matter how good this philosophy might sound, we cannot follow it. It is generally considered that we must maximize our wealth in order to give our people a better standard of living.
There are those who say we should import no energy into Canada and should not export energy in any form. The example I gave in respect of electricity and the arrangement between Manitoba and its counterpart in the United States is not very compatible with such a view. We must recognize that there are some problems involved in adopting such a stance. There is the matter of the scale of economics involved in bringing into supply the energy we shall need for our own use. This may well be too large a problem for our relatively small domestic market to sustain. We could incur substantial economic penalties. One example might be the Mackenzie Valley. It is obvious that the Mackenzie Valley gas pipeline can only be tapped in the immediate future if the Americans are involved. Then, again, we wish at present to export both resources and technology in many areas. We want to export uranium, Uranium, Candu technology and nuclear-generated electricity all fall into this category.
It seems to me that we also must realize that national interest must be put above regional interests, and this poses a real problem. It is obviously very difficult to reconcile the national interest with regional interests. The province of Saskatchewan, which for many years was a

have-not province, having suddenly become the owner of a scarce resource found that it could not capitalize from it as it should in a purely economic way. There must be recognition of the fact that provincial rights regarding the ownership of resources should not be changed unilaterally by the federal government. If this bill is to change the right of the provinces to their resources, the provinces will find that they will lose in importance to their own people, that they will be diminished and eventually will become not much more than city governments.
We must also accept the fact that our economic growth must be maintained. The important question that this bill tackles is who should exercise control over the development of resources and how the benefits flowing from them should be distributed. In other words, how should our energy resources be used to maximize our financial potential: should they be used to subsidize the manufacturing industry in its various forms? I think this is the central question and one that is causing those who live in the remote parts of the country serious thought with regard to the government's thrust.
There are those who suggest that manufacturing activity has been hampered in Canada for many years, that it has been insignificant and inefficient. I think it is fair to say that without the great wealth which our energy and natural resources have brought us, the manufacturing industry could not have provided Canada with the high level of income that it enjoys. Wealth distribution is necessary. Also, it must be remembered that the province of Saskatchewan has been prevented from reaping the benefits of its resources. Finally, we must ask ourselves whether we want to have a market economy in control of our petroleum resources. I think this is probably the key to the problem. Traditionally, Canada has had a market economy in the oil industry. Personally, I have had to make the decision whether to use electricity, gas or oil. I chose heating oil because it afforded greater flexibility and was the best choice for my purpose. But will the price of $6.50 set by the government be enough?
We must remember that when the economics of oil are considered, $200 or $300 spent in the Middle East will produce one barrel of oil a day. In the North Sea, $25 spent will produce a barrel of oil a day, whereas we require $10,000 to produce a barrel of oil if the tar sands are exploited. In the United States, new oil brings upward of $10 a day. It attracts Canadian companies and Canadian money, mainly the independents which are considered to be our particular contribution to the oil industry, Will the price of $6.50 for oil bring them back? The fact that oil reserves are being reduced by half a billion barrels a year-that is, the traditional, conventional oil wells-and that we have not had a strike in many years must not be forgotten.
Oil drilling statistics indicate that Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have reduced their oil drilling activities so far this year. Obviously, this will pose a significant problem. There is no point in saying that we have found a solution in setting the price of oil at $6.50 a barrel. So long as the Americans will pay $4 for it, or so long as the Arabs hold it up, the fact is that this will be a continuing problem. Will the entry of the government into the market enhance activity within the oil producing
Petroleum Administration Act
sector of our economy and provide us with the required amounts of oil for the future?

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF EXPORT CHARGE, COMPENSATION FOR OIL IMPORT COSTS AND REGULATION OF PRICE OF CANADIAN CRUDE IN INTERPROVINCIAL AND EXPORT TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not long ago that I rose to speak on an oil bill. At that time it was the oil allocation bill and I rose to speak on it because the government was asking for extraordinary powers to deal with a so-called crisis which I felt was a transportation crisis rather than one of supply.
Today we look at Bill C-18 which is to impose an export tax on crude oil and provide subsidy funds to the non-producing areas. Again I see that the government is asking for extraordinary powers which I do not think we should grant them. Already the government possesses many of these powers under the National Energy Board Act and other existing legislation. However, as the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) said, the government is like a fox in the crowd, trying to sneak in some powers which perhaps were not considered at the provincial-federal conference which was held recently.
As we have said before, we would not have too much objection to passing parts I and IV of the bill, as the hon. member explained when speaking about the history of the export tax and its necessity after the price freeze on oil. But why do we need to grant the government powers under parts II and III?
I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for being able to get the ten provinces together and come up with some agreement. Before I go on to a close scrutiny of the clauses in the bill, I would like to speak about a group of people who are caught in the middle. They do not have much to do with the producing provinces or with the federal government so far as the export tax or the subsidy is concerned. These are our Indian or native people.
On numerous occasions I have spoken to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern development (Mr. Chretien) respecting the return of the export tax to the Indian people. But before continuing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I was quite concerned just a few weeks ago when it came to my attention that even if the price of oil were to increase to $6.50 a barrel, the royalty rate to Indian people on their reserves was set at $4 a barrel, and there would have to be substantial changes made in the schedules to the legislation so that they could collect increased royalties and so that the oil companies would not receive the additonal $2.50 per barrel. I commend both ministers for having regulations changed whereby the Indian people could increase their royalty rates above those established under the schedules to take advantage of the increase in price from $4 to $6.50.
So far as the export tax is concerned, I find that although the federal government has been collecting this money it has not allowed the Indian people to take any advantage from it. From October, 1973, until April 1, 1974, a large amount of this money has accumulated in the federal treasury and has not been redistributed to the Indian bands. Perhaps there are some reasons for this. There may be problems involved in giving the total of this

April 8, 1974
Petroleum Administration Act
amount of money back to the Indian bands, or even half, according to the precedent set under the previous arrangement whereby Saskatchewan and Alberta got half.
It is something the federal government should look into because future development of oil reserves in the tar sands will not do the Indian people as much good as such development will do for all the rest of Canada. Perhaps we should look at this money as an investment in the ability of these people to look after their own affairs, and in turn to invest it in opportunities for their future. Perhaps they would be able to set up certain industries with it, buy machinery, set up agricultural feed lots, or invest in the lumber and mineral industries. I call on the minister to make an announcement respecting the return of the export tax to the native people as soon as possible, because they could take better advantage of it in late spring and during the summer to build houses or to make investments in their own industries.
Part I of the bill deals with the export tax. I must echo the words of some other hon. members who have said they feel this export tax is setting a dangerous precedent. I have some concern that we may face reciprocal action by other nations in the future, particularly the United States. We have already seen that the example of the OPEC nations in setting the price of international oil is being followed in other areas. Take the case of fishmeal in South America. Some of the nations there have taken a good look at the OPEC pricing of oil and have set higher prices for their fishmeal, even though the price at which this product was previously being sold to Canada gave everybody a reasonable profit. We also find that bauxite from Trinidad and South America is demanding a much higher price in recent days.
What will happen to the world situation if countries start hoarding resources which are not in plentiful supply? How will the third world nations afford those resources and meet the wishes of their peoples to reach the standards of living enjoyed by Canada, the United States, Europe and, more recently, by Japan and a number of other countries? As I say, I am quite concerned about the precedent we are setting in taking advantage of other countries.
Premier Lougheed is a good Canadian who, with his government, has done everything possible during the past year to get oil from Alberta to eastern Canada, shipping it across the mountains and through the Panama Canal. In a recent speech immediately after the conference in Ottawa he said he was pleased with the negotiated price. Perhaps I might outline some of the things he said. I quote:
I would now like to outline the reasons why we concluded that an average price of $6.50 per barrel is in the public interest of Alberta at this time:
The price is approximately the same as the average United States domestic crude oil price which is a matter of significance in terms of continued exploratory drilling for conventional crude oil in Alberta and Canada.
The point has been made many times that we have perhaps only ten to 15 years' supply of conventional oil in Canada, and the industry will require at least ten years' lead time to enable the tar sands to make up the difference in future demand, or perhaps to find more conventional oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan, offshore or perhaps in the Arctic. Adequate incentives must be available to the oil

companies so that they will continue to explore for oil here rather than going to other countries such as the United States or to the North Sea oil fields. Premier Lougheed also said:
Such a price at this time in our view provides adequate encouragement for continued interest in future oil sands projects and should permit the Great Canadian Oil Sands plant to start to make up for previous losses. Syncrude did not anticipate last August that such a price would be realized until 1984.
The instability of the OPEC pricing structure is well known, and a higher price until the world pricing situation has stabilized is considered ill-advised for now. United States energy chief, William Simon, predicted earlier this week that world market pressures would force down the price of oil.
I have heard the question asked by eastern Canadians: What is Alberta going to do with all the money it will receive from increased royalties on the oil it is producing? I think Albertans should make it clear that they are not going to stand forever for the export of their raw materials and resources to other parts of Canada, or to other parts of the world, to be manufactured there and then shipped back to Alberta, with Albertans having to pay the transportation for their return. In Alberta we want to provide industry for the people who are coming there. I see you looking at the clock, Mr. Speaker, so perhaps I might continue another day.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STRIKE BY FIREFIGHTERS AT VANCOUVER AIRPORT-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
AIR TRANSPORT-STRIKE BY FIREFIGHTERS AT VANCOUVER AIRPORT-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext:
Tonight, Mr. Speaker, I want to talk a little about the situation in British Columbia where we have a strike not only at Vancouver international airport but at all the airports in the province, a strike that I think could have been avoided if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) had taken a little more care in dealing with people in that area. I would like to read a telegram sent to these ministers a number of days before the strike took place. It reads:
Owing to the deterioration of labour morale in the federal civil service of western Canada and possibly all of Canada, and after eight years of fruitless bargaining, we find ourselves in a position where we, the airport firefighters of western Canada, must withdraw our services for an indefinite period to study our worsening plight. At present we are over $4,000 per year behind our local counterparts. There have been abnormally large staff resignations in western Canada. One airport in British Columbia plans mass resignation if immediate action by Treasury Board is not taken to guarantee federal government fire-fighters parity with outside counterparts. If the trickle of resignations of the present is not sandbagged, the floods of tomorrow will destory the very foundations of all the civil service. Treasury Board must be made
April 8, 1974

aware of the dangerous trend. There must be an immediate reversal of their inhuman, indifferent, and unfair bargaining philosophy.
Fire Fighter Action Committee 658 Miller Road Richmond, B.C.
I am happy to see the President of the Treasury Board here tonight, Mr. Speaker. Five days before the strike took place, his office was called and asked if he would go out and talk to these men because they were concerned about what was happening; the regional bargainers had not been able to settle the problems. That phone call from the firefighting committee has not been answered yet. I should like to refer to page 852 of Hansard of March 25, 1974, and quote the President of the Treasury Board on the subject of regional pay policy which the firefighters are seeking. He said:
In the case of regional pay policy, the government for years has taken the position that it will not be a leader in matters of pay and salary but will follow the pattern set by what is generally known in this country as the private sector. Given the choice of trying to equate the pay of the public service to that of the private sector on a national level or on a regional level, the government must, for common sense reasons, use a regional basis.
I would say to the President of the Treasury Board that that is exactly what the firefighters at Vancouver are looking for. I have been talking to them on a regular basis since before the strike began, and I know they have tried very hard to contact the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Transport to ask them to come to British Columbia so they can explain their problems. This morning I telephoned the office of the Minister of Transport to say that I had a proposal from the firefighters on strike that I thought could end it tomorrow. The strikers were asking that the bargaining be done in Vancouver, not with the union in Ottawa which they do not think is doing a good job for them. They were asking for reassurance that the government is willing to talk wage parity with the municipalities in British Columbia and that the talks be based on settling the problems on a regional basis.
I told the minister's executive assistant that these people would be available to discuss this proposal before the House sat today. The members of the union had asked me to attend the meeting because I am the member of parliament for the area which has the largest airport in British Columbia, Vancouver international airport. I have yet to receive a call from the minister's office. In the House this afternoon the minister rose and said, "I was told a couple of minutes ago that my people have landed in Vancouver-"

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STRIKE BY FIREFIGHTERS AT VANCOUVER AIRPORT-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext: Which minister?

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STRIKE BY FIREFIGHTERS AT VANCOUVER AIRPORT-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport. I can just about quote him verbatim. He said, "A couple of minutes ago my people landed in Vancouver to talk to the strikers". At a quarter to ten tonight, Ottawa time, I spoke to the strikers and they told me they have yet to hear from the people who landed there this afternoon. The conduct of the minister and of the government in ignoring these people in Vancouver leaves a lot to be desired. If they do not get this problem settled we could have strikes all across the country, which will mean a lot of difficulty for
Adjournment Debate
many people. I had a telephone call from a man who came back from Mexico last night. He complained that he went through four Customs' stops. First they were checked in Mexico, then in Seattle, which passed them to Blaine, then the Canadian Customs checked them, and again at Vancouver international airport. This creates great inconvenience for the people of British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think this government or the minister concerned are making a sincere effort. It is time the ministers went out there to talk to the people, because it is obvious that this dispute cannot be settled at the regional level. The Minister of Transport and the President of the Treasury Board are the gentlemen who have to settle the strike; it is part of their job. They must find out what the real problems are in British Columbia. We hear of western alienation, and this is one of the reasons. Ministers send other people out instead of going themselves to settle the problem. What else can one say but that the ministers should get out there and settle the strike? I know we will now hear from the government about all the work they have done. They have not done a damn thing, because airplanes still are not landing in Vancouver.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-STRIKE BY FIREFIGHTERS AT VANCOUVER AIRPORT-REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last few words of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) are normal for members of the opposition. They draw conclusions before they even hear an answer. The hon. member made reference to a parliamentary secretary. I want to make it clear that he did not speak to me today. He might have spoken to another parliamentary secretary, but certainly not to me.
With regard to the hon. member's question, the Ministry of Transport firefighters in Vancouver and at other airports in British Columbia walked off the job at 8 a.m. on Friday, April 5. Prior to this walk-out we had engaged in numerous discussions with the leaders of the firefighters in Vancouver in an effort to dissuade them from this course of action. These employees are represented by the Public Service Alliance of Canada which was certified under the Public Service Staff Relations Act on August 2, 1967 as their bargaining agent.
The collective agreement governing their terms and conditions of employment, including rates of pay, expired March 31, 1974. Bargaining for a new collective agreement with Treasury Board began February 20 and several negotiating sessions have taken place since then. The members of this group have selected compulsory arbitration as the method to settle the dispute if they are unable to reach agreement in direct negotiations.
The heart of the current problem is that the employees in B.C., especially in Vancouver, are seeking what is known as regional rates of pay and the bargaining agent, through its convention, has a policy of national rates of pay. Therefore, as you can appreciate, it is not a dispute with the Ministry of Transport but, rather, a difference of opinion between some members of the bargaining unit and the organization that represents them. The Ministry of Transport is caught in the middle.
In collective bargaining for most parts of the public service, Treasury Board acts as the employer, and negotiations for the firefighters in the public service are between
1266

April 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Treasury Board and the Public Service Alliance of Canada. Those who are familiar with labour legislation will realize that an employer must deal with the certified bargaining agent and he cannot make separate arrangements with parts of the bargaining unit. In fact, most labour legislation contains specific prohibitions in respect of such action. In the Public Service Staff Relations Act, section 8, subsection (1) reads as follows:
No person who is employed in a managerial or confidential capacity, whether or not he is acting on behalf of the employer, shall participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of an employee organization or the representation of employees by such an organization.
We have attempted to convince the employees concerned that the only lawful course of action must be through their bargaining agent and we are prohibited by law passed by this parliament from pursuing any other course in this regard. We have attempted, and are continuing efforts to persuade employees that this is the proper way to deal with their problems and are doing everything within our power to facilitate such action.

subtopic: FINANCE-RESULT OF COURT ACTION AGAINST PERSON DISCOUNTING GOVERNMENT CHEQUES-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT OF SMALL LOANS ACT
FINANCE-RESULT OF COURT ACTION AGAINST PERSON DISCOUNTING GOVERNMENT CHEQUES-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT OF SMALL LOANS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for three years now I have been raising in this House the question of government action to control the practice of discounting operations on government cheques. On March 19 I asked the following question of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray):
Is the government contemplating amendments to the Small Loans Act which would bring within its ambit this kind of transaction which is essentially a lending operation?
The minister replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, this is being examined.
After three years, the government is still studying the question. At least when I raised the question initially with the minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission, three years ago, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), I got some action. There were some changes in UIC regulations which prevented the assignment of unemployment insurance cheques to discounters which diminished, if it did not eliminate, the practice of discounting unemployment insurance cheques. Beyond that, the Superintendent of Insurance carried out an investigation to see if the practice of discounting government cheques was in violation of federal statutes, and a discounter was taken to court. The discounter won the case, as I was informed on March 19 by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), a fact which suggests to me that legislation is required. If the government was serious about dealing with the problem, it would have had legislation prepared to handle the problem in the eventuality that the court ruled against the Crown's case.
Discounting is the practice of providing someone with a sum of money on the basis of their having proof that they are entitled to receive a like or greater sum, and assigning that entitlement to the person providing the immediate cash. Thus, a correctly completed income tax form indicating a rebate due can, if the right to the receipt of the

rebate cheque is assigned, provide the means of obtaining immediate cash. In the types of operation I wish to stop, the amount of cash received is usually 30 to 40 per cent less than the actual amount of the rebate. If computed as interest on an annual basis, that 30 to 40 per cent discount represents usurious interest rates amounting to 1,000 per cent or more when one considers that the lender of the money has only to wait a few days, or up to a couple of months at most, to be reimbursed.
The difficulty in controlling the situation is evident when one attempts to define what this practice of discounting actually involves. If it is, in effect, a lending operation then the powers the federal government possesses under section 91 of the BNA Act to control banking, bills of exchange and interest rates would come into play. Thus, the logical step would seem to be that of amending the Small Loans Act to bring the practice of discounting government cheques of less than a certain amount under its provisions, thereby restricting the effective interest rate charged to a maximum of 2 per cent per month. This is what my bill, C-257, now on the order paper for the second parliament and the third straight session attempts to do.
If, on the other hand, the evidence of entitlement to receive money in the future from the government can be considered to be a piece of personal property liable to sale, then regulation of the amount of discount to be allowed might well fall under section 92 of the British North America Act which lays down the right of a province to deal with contract law.
The area may be regarded as an obscure one and thus best dealt with by means of federal and provincial action. I fail to see why the federal government should fear to take the lead. There is a problem, as the figures show. In 1972, the number of rebates discounted in British Columbia amounted 5,273; in Alberta, 6,391; in Saskatchewan, 2,406; in Manitoba, 1,269; in Ontario, 543; in Quebec, 477; and in Nova Scotia, 93. Thus, more than 14,000 income tax refunds were discounted by sharp operators posing as tax preparers. The total value of the refunds claimed amounted to some $3.2 million. How much will it be in 1973 and in 1974?
The effect of federal inertia has been to force British Columbia to take unilateral action to deal with the situation by using its licensing power to force loan sharks out of business. Persons seeking a licence to prepare income tax returns who also engage in discounting might not get a licence. Manitoba, I understand, is contemplating similar steps. No one, I believe, would consider such legislation to be good legislation. It is arbitrary, it sets no standards and thus it is open to abuse. But it sets no standards and thus it is open to abuse. But in the absence of federal action, indeed, in the light of federal recommendations that this is the action which provinces concerned about the problem should take, there is little else a province can do.
It would seem to me that the federal government should immediately introduce legislation bringing the practice in this country under the Small Loans Act and that it should immediately seek concurrent legislation from the provinces validating the right of the federal government to
April 8, 1974

take such action in this specific case. Only in this way can we finally rid this country of a despicable practice in a manner which is completely in accordance with the concepts of due process and equality under the law.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: FINANCE-RESULT OF COURT ACTION AGAINST PERSON DISCOUNTING GOVERNMENT CHEQUES-POSSIBLE AMENDMENT OF SMALL LOANS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my view the hon. member greatly underestimates the legal problems and constitutional complexities underlying the very real problem to which be referred.
I completely agree with him on the fact that there are some absolutely unforgivable abuses, and he gave us a few cases, but I must tell him that so far, in view of the few cases of jurisprudence, the courts have considered that discounting of a government cheque was not a loan but essentially a transfer of credit and, in that respect, I think the hon. member will agree with me that provincial jurisdiction is much more real than federal jurisdiction. In my view, the government of the province that he represents so well in the House could do more since transfer of debt comes first under provincial jurisdiction.
In any event, I want to assure him, even if he is listening with some skepticism, that all federal government departments involved in this matter-National Revenue, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Justice and Finance- are now working on a solution to this problem without infringing the Canadian constitution. Then, how can this cheque discounting problem which he is referring to and which has lead to absolutely regrettable abuses, not to mention usurious rates, be brought under federal jurisdiction? I want the hon. member to know that it is not a very simple matter, but I agree with him that we absolutely must put a stop to such abuses.
Another related problem must be taken into consideration; we should not tend to restrict unduly the freedom of the Canadian people.
In certain cases, some of them may discount their cheque for reasons which are their own, and I do not think the philosophy of our government system allows the administration to decide for its citizens what is good for them; this, of course, is true within certain limits, which presumes equality between lendee and lender, an equality which is often lacking, I must agree with the hon. member.
I should, however, like to thank him for having raised this problem and to assure him that the Departments of Justice, Finance, Consumer and Corporate Affairs and National Revenue are working towards finding a solution within the framework of the Canadian constitution.

subtopic: ENERGY-HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA-REASON FOR PURCHASE
ENERGY-HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA-REASON FOR PURCHASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the gradual unfolding of the story of the government's handling of the heating oil purchased last winter has produced an incredibly sorry picture of incompetence, bungling, and indeed suspicions of serious conflict of interest.
Last winter after the Middle East war and the Arab oil embargo came into effect there was, naturally, quite a bit of concern about the security of supply of oil to the
Adjournment Debate
eastern part of Canada which relies on imported oil. The government was obviously confused and uncertain, to put it mildly. It appointed a group called the technical advisory committee on petroleum supplies, consisting of representatives from industry and several government departments. Based supposedly on the recommendation of this committee, the government decided that there would be a shortfall in supply this winter of between 75,000 and
200,000	barrels of oil a day. Although questioned extensively, the government steadfastly refused to provide proof, or even knowledgeable evidence, that this was a reasonable estimate of the shortfall.
To my knowledge, only one company, namely Imperial Oil, which incidentally does not rely on Middle East crude, publicly suggested that this estimate was valid. Many other companies indicated they would look after their own customers and would do so without government assistance. Of course, we later learned that the government had not taken into account the supplies that would be available from the Newfoundland refinery at Come-By-Chance, sometimes known as the Shaheen refinery, supplies from which would have been available by the end of December last.
We now know that on November 9, 1973, the Department of Supply and Services contracted with Canadian Fuel Marketers-incidentally, a member of this technical advisory committee-to purchase 20,000 metric tons of oil from Roumania and 40,000 metric tons from Shell International Curacao refinery in the Caribbean at a price to be arranged. It is interesting to note that on November 15, 1973, my colleague, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden), asked the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) with what company he had arranged this contract. His exact words were, as reported at page 7819 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask if the minister is in a position to say to whom he has given this blank cheque?
I doubt that my friend the hon. member for Calgary South realized just how prophetic that question was, because last week in the miscellaneous estimates committee the minister finally acknowledged that the average delivered price paid for 26 million gallons of oil purchased was an astronomical 79 cents per gallon. The price paid for the Roumanian portion was an unbelievable 99 Vi cents per gallon. Asked why he had made such a terrible deal for the Roumanian oil, the Minister of Supply and Services said it was part of the deal which enabled the government to purchase cheaper, but still tremendously overpriced, Caribbean oil. Yet in committee officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, upon whose advice the Minister of Supply and Services claimed he relied, stated that the Roumanian deal was quite separate and was undertaken on its merits.
Which story is true, Mr. Speaker? If the true story is that of the Minister of Supply and Services, then why would Canadian Fuel Marketers, a company owned by Shell International, insist that Canada buy oil from the Roumanian State Oil Company with no apparent profit motive on their part? If officials of the Energy, Mines and Resources Department are right, then why did the govern-
1268

April 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
ment buy such incredibly expensive oil, evidently the highest priced heating oil sold this winter or sold ever, for that matter?
These questions need answering, Mr. Speaker. This oil cost the Canadian taxpayers $20.5 million and has a current commercial value of less than one-third that amount. In other words, this deal has cost us more than did the outfitting of the Bonaventure, that other example of government bungling and incompetence. The time has come for the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) to have the Auditor General conduct a full-scale investigation into this blatant misuse of public funds.
There are a number of questions that need answering, including the question of possible conflict of interest, the question of proper or improper business practices of the Department of Supply and Services, and the question of the competence of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which evidently supplied the background information.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-HEATING OIL PURCHASED BY GOVERNMENT FROM ROUMANIA-REASON FOR PURCHASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) ranting away in his rather ugly manner about this question for the last ten days or so there are several conclusions to be drawn. The first is that while members of this House, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), were saying on November 5 that they were concerned about the situation in respect of oil in eastern Canada, and that this government should go out and purchase oil on the market to cover the shortfall that was evidently going to occur, the hon. member for Calgary Centre would have opposed that at the time.
At the same time, he would have said we should not have exercised the contracts on behalf of the eastern Canadian consumer of heating oil and would oppose that as well. That kind of improvidence, that kind of heartlessness and that kind of narrow parochialism which has always distinguished the hon. member for Calgary Centre in this House is the kind of attitude that I suppose more than any other will damage the relations between one group of Canadians and another. I regret that this kind of ugly attitude is represented in this House. We have to put
up with that member with patience, but I must say with regret.
What is the fact of the matter? The fact of the matter is that a substantial portion of the heating oil used in eastern Canada for many years has come from imported products. With international markets tightening up, it was important that the Canadian consumer should be protected in this way. Because of the dramatic increase in the international price due to the shortfall on the international market and the embargo, importers were not in a position to import this oil; therefore the government moved in to protect the eastern Canadian consumer by taking an assignment of the contract so as to open up, in the first place, the Roumanian market for the purpose of access and also to pick up existing contracts from the Caribbean.
The hon. member says the government was uncertain as to the amount of this shortfall. Of course the government was uncertain, as was every intelligent person. Could any intelligent person predict that we would have a cold or an average winter this year, or a milder winter as it turned out to be? Could any intelligent person at that time predict whether the Arab embargo would continue in the way it did, or that production would be reduced progressively by 5 per cent a month? Of course not.
It is all very well to have such magnificent hindsight and talk as the hon. member has, now that we have come successfully through the winter and that eastern Canada did not suffer from the shortfall. Now we have a series of false allegations being made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre and by the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour). We have had allegations that the oil was not up to snuff, that there was a conflict of interest and that it cost too much because it was paid for at market price on the international market.
I would have to say that the important thing from the standpoint of the government is not to take chances with the people as the hon. member for Calgary South and the hon. member for Calgary Centre are prepared to do. A responsible government will protect the Canadian people against the very worst possible anticipated risks. It is in that framework that we acted to protect the people. I would far sooner have prepared for the worst, and have the best, than to have acted as the hon. member for Calgary Centre suggests, to have hoped for the best and wound up with the worst.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.29 p.m.
